meta.blurb: Four hours a day, no destination, no hurry. Thoreau called it sauntering, and he said he could not stay healthy or cheerful without it. Follow his short essay into the swamps and see why he trusted the wild.
meta.bible: Henry David Thoreau: American writer and naturalist of the nineteenth century, born in Concord, Massachusetts, in 1817; died on 6 May 1862 aged 44 of tuberculosis. Walking: his essay on the art of walking and the value of wild nature, printed in The Atlantic Monthly in June 1862, soon after his death; it grew out of lectures he gave in the early 1850s. Concord: his home town in Massachusetts; the Concord River, the Great Meadows and Fair Haven Hill are places he walked. Harvard: the college he finished in 1837. Surveyor: one of his trades; the others were teaching and pencil-making in his family's business. Ralph Waldo Emerson: his older friend and neighbour in Concord. Sophia: his sister, who helped look after his papers. Walden Pond: the pond near Concord where he lived in a small cabin for about two years from 1845. Walden: his book about it, printed in 1854. Maine, Katahdin, Cape Cod and Chesuncook: places he visited and wrote about. Lyceum: the Concord hall where he gave lectures. Sleepy Hollow: the Concord cemetery where he is buried. Hawthorne and Alcott: writers buried near him. Saunter, Sauntering, Saunterer and Saunterers: Thoreau's word for walking slowly and freely with no goal; he gives two stories for where the word comes from, and they are guesses. Walker Errant: Thoreau's name for a knight who goes on foot. Holy Land: the Sainte Terre of the old pilgrims, Sainte-Terrer. Crusade and Crusaders: the medieval holy wars; Peter the Hermit preached the First Crusade. Wildness: his word for the free, untamed life of nature, which he values highly. Swamp: the wet, dark wood he loves to visit. Sphagnum, Andromeda, Rhodora and Azalea: plants of the swamp. Pilgrims, Knights, Chevalier, Walkers. Atlantic and Pacific: the oceans. Atlantis, Hesperides and Elysian Fields: legendary western lands of the ancient poets; Plato wrote of Atlantis and nobody has found it. Lethe and Styx: the rivers of forgetting and of the dead in Greek myth. Old World and New World. Oregon: then the far west of the country. Michaux: a French botanist who travelled west of the Alleghanies in 1802. Berkeley: George Berkeley, Irish bishop whose verse says empire moves westward; Heracles: Greek hero. Columbus, Vespucius, Menu, Moses, Chaucer, Wordsworth: names Thoreau uses. Romulus and Remus: the founders of Rome in the old tale, said to have been nursed by a she-wolf. Homer, Confucius, Hamlet, Iliad, Robin Hood, Chaucer, Spenser, Milton, Shakespeare, Scriptures: names from literature. Lake Poets: Wordsworth and his circle. Humboldt: Alexander von Humboldt, German naturalist. Greece, Empire, England. Reformer: Thoreau's name for John the Baptist. Europe, America, Asia, Africa, Rome, Latin, Greek. Muir: John Muir, nature writer who founded the Sierra Club in 1892. Wilderness Act: American law of 1964 protecting wild land. Latin sayings quoted by Thoreau: light comes from the East, fruit from the West; walkers are born, not made. Key quotations are real and short: Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free; and In Wildness is the preservation of the World. Thoreau was a writer and not a doctor; the health remarks are his own opinions. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: calm, curious, a little humorous and very outdoors; Thoreau's own opinions are always marked as his.

beats.scene: Thoreau strides along a country lane near Concord in morning light
beats.summary: Henry David Thoreau, a writer of Concord, Massachusetts, spent much of his life walking the lanes, fields and woods near his home.

beats.scene: A quiet New England village with a white church, a river and meadows
beats.summary: Concord was a small farming village with meadows, orchards and a slow river; Thoreau was born there in 1817.

beats.scene: A young man in a dark coat climbs old brick college steps
beats.summary: After finishing at Harvard in 1837 he did not follow the usual career path and came home to Concord.

beats.scene: A workbench with pencils in rows and a surveyor's chain on the wall
beats.summary: He made a plain living from his family's pencil business, from surveying land and from odd jobs, which left him free hours to roam.

beats.scene: Two men in coats walk and talk along a field edge in autumn
beats.summary: His older friend and neighbour Ralph Waldo Emerson, a famous writer, encouraged his writing, and the two often walked and talked together.

beats.scene: A small wooden cabin beside a quiet pond among pine trees
beats.summary: In 1845 he built a cabin at Walden Pond on land Emerson owned, and lived there for about two years.

beats.scene: A man writes in a notebook while sitting on a log in the woods
beats.summary: He kept a journal for most of his adult life, noting birds, flowers, weather and the dates when leaves first appeared.

beats.scene: A lecture hall with a speaker at a lamplit desk and rows of listeners
beats.summary: A few years after leaving the pond he gave talks on walking and wild nature, which grew into the essay.

beats.scene: A thin man at a desk by a window, papers piled beside him
beats.summary: Weakened by tuberculosis, he kept revising his essays, and he died at home in Concord on 6 May 1862, aged 44.

beats.scene: Magazine pages lie open beside a pair of worn leather boots
beats.summary: A month later, in June 1862, the Atlantic Monthly printed his essay Walking, and this book follows it step by step.

beats.scene: Thoreau stands at a lectern, one hand raised, in a plain hall
beats.summary: He opens by saying he wishes to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness.

beats.scene: A town hall with a flag, and open meadows stretching behind it
beats.summary: He sets the freedom of nature against a freedom that is only civil, the kind that laws, votes and good manners give.

beats.scene: A small human figure stands among tall trees and rolling hills
beats.summary: He wants to see a person as an inhabitant, even a part and parcel, of Nature, rather than only as a member of society.

beats.scene: A speaker smiles at a crowd, one finger raised for emphasis
beats.summary: He admits he wants to make an extreme statement, because a bold claim is more memorable than a mild one.

beats.scene: A church, a schoolhouse and a town hall stand side by side
beats.summary: There are enough champions of civilization, he says; the minister, the school committee and everyone present will speak for that.

beats.scene: A wooden fence at the village edge with a wild wood beyond
beats.summary: He is not against towns or schools; he wants his listeners to remember what lies beyond the last fence.

beats.scene: A walker steps over a low stone wall into a meadow
beats.summary: For him, walking is the plainest way to step out of society's rules without breaking any of them.

beats.scene: A man with a stick stops on a hill and looks out
beats.summary: He says he has met only one or two people who truly understood the art of walking.

beats.scene: A walker moves slowly through a wood, head up, eyes wide
beats.summary: Such a person has what he calls a genius for sauntering, which is quite different from marching to a place.

beats.scene: An old dictionary lies open beside a walking stick on a table
beats.summary: Then he asks where the odd word saunter comes from and offers two stories.

beats.scene: Ragged wanderers on a medieval road, one pointing at a far hill
beats.summary: The first story says saunter comes from idle wanderers of the Middle Ages who begged and said they were going to the Holy Land.

beats.scene: Village children point at a ragged traveller and shout together
beats.summary: Children, he says, would cry out that there goes a Sainte-Terrer, a Holy-Lander, and the name wore down into saunterer.

beats.scene: A traveller with a bundle and staff stands on a village green
beats.summary: Those who never reach the Holy Land are mere idlers, he jokes, but those who do go are saunterers in the good sense.

beats.scene: A lone walker crosses open country with no house in sight
beats.summary: The second story says saunter comes from sans terre, French for without land, so a saunterer has no fixed home.

beats.scene: A figure sits on a hilltop with a whole valley spread below
beats.summary: Having no particular home means being at home everywhere, and that is the secret of successful sauntering.

beats.scene: A man sits in a dim room while a bright field waits outside
beats.summary: He says that a man who sits still in his house all the time may be the greatest vagrant of all.

beats.scene: A winding river curls across a green valley toward distant water
beats.summary: The saunterer is no more a vagrant than a meandering river, which is all the while seeking the shortest course to the sea.

beats.scene: A preacher with a staff speaks to a crowd on a hill
beats.summary: He prefers the first story: every walk is a sort of crusade, preached by some Peter the Hermit within us.

beats.scene: A pilgrim's staff and a scallop shell rest on a stone step
beats.summary: The real Peter the Hermit was a preacher of the eleventh century who stirred crowds to set out for the Holy Land.

beats.scene: A map of the Holy Land lies beside a walker's muddy boots
beats.summary: For Thoreau the Holy Land is not only a place on a map; it is whatever wild country a walker sets out to find.

beats.scene: A few walkers set off at dawn, looking back at the village
beats.summary: He says that even the walkers of his day are faint-hearted crusaders who take on no persevering, never-ending enterprise.

beats.scene: A walker comes home at dusk to a lit window and a fireside
beats.summary: Our expeditions are only tours, he says, and by evening we come round again to the old hearth-side we set out from.

beats.scene: A footpath loops through a wood and returns to the same gate
beats.summary: Half the walk, he observes, is merely retracing our steps.

beats.scene: A lone walker on a long road heads toward distant mountains
beats.summary: He wishes we could walk in the spirit of undying adventure, never meaning to return.

beats.scene: A small carved casket with a heart on it rests on a table
beats.summary: He imagines setting out so completely that we would send home only our embalmed hearts, as relics for our desolate kingdoms.

beats.scene: A family waves from a garden gate as a traveller walks away
beats.summary: The first condition for a true walk is to be ready to leave father, mother, brother, sister, wife, child and friends, and never see them again.

beats.scene: A table holds paid bills, a folded will and a closed account book
beats.summary: The second is to have paid your debts, made your will and settled your affairs, so that you are a free man.

beats.scene: A walker with an easy smile stands in an open doorway
beats.summary: These demands are half a joke; what he truly asks is that a walker's mind be free of worry and duty.

beats.scene: Two walkers with sticks and hats stand like knights on a hilltop
beats.summary: He and his walking companion like to imagine themselves knights of a new, or rather an old, order: not riders but Walkers.

beats.scene: A lone walker stands apart from a church, a courthouse and a crowd
beats.summary: The Walker Errant, he says, is a sort of fourth estate, outside of Church and State and People.

beats.scene: A few villagers at their doors watch a lone walker pass by
beats.summary: He feels that he and his companion almost alone practise this noble art, though most townsmen say they would like to walk but cannot.

beats.scene: A heavy purse sits beside a stopped clock on a table
beats.summary: No wealth can buy the leisure, freedom and independence that are the capital in this profession, he says.

beats.scene: A small child takes first steps across a sunlit meadow
beats.summary: It requires a direct dispensation from Heaven to become a walker, and he jokes in Latin that a walker is born, not made.

beats.scene: A man strides through open woods at noon, sun on his shoulders
beats.summary: He says he cannot keep his health and spirits unless he spends at least four hours a day sauntering in the woods and fields.

beats.scene: A hat rests on a stump beside an empty hillside path
beats.summary: He means four hours absolutely free from every worldly engagement: no errands, no appointments and no work.

beats.scene: A row of shopkeepers sit with crossed legs in a dim shop
beats.summary: Mechanics and shopkeepers sit in their shops all day, as if legs were made only for sitting, and he says they deserve credit for bearing it.

beats.scene: A tool lies in a damp cellar, its metal blotched with rust
beats.summary: He cannot stay in his room for a single day without acquiring some rust.

beats.scene: Low sun above dark trees as a man hurries out of his door
beats.summary: When he steals out at the eleventh hour, too late to redeem the day, he feels he has committed a sin to be atoned for.

beats.scene: A clerk bends over a ledger while a bright window shows green trees
beats.summary: He is astonished at the endurance, and even the moral insensibility, of neighbours who stay in shops and offices all day.

beats.scene: A man hoes beans in a small field beside a cabin
beats.summary: He arranged his life for this freedom: at Walden he reckoned that about six weeks of work a year could pay his way.

beats.scene: A walker stands deep in the woods, frowning, hands behind him
beats.summary: Sometimes he walks a mile into the woods in body without getting there in spirit, and it alarms him.

beats.scene: A man leaves a busy village behind him on an afternoon path
beats.summary: On his afternoon walk he wants to forget his morning occupations and his obligations to society.

beats.scene: A walker in a wood looks back over his shoulder at far roofs
beats.summary: Sometimes he cannot shake off the village: the thought of some work runs in his head, and he is out of his senses.

beats.scene: A walker pauses with eyes closed, listening to birdsong in a wood
beats.summary: On his walks he would gladly return to his senses and truly see, hear and smell the world around him.

beats.scene: Thoreau pauses at a stream, looking closely at the running water
beats.summary: What business has he in the woods, he asks, if he is thinking of something outside the woods?

beats.scene: A church, a school and a courthouse look tiny beneath a huge sky
beats.summary: Church and State and school, trade and commerce, even politics, take up very little space in the landscape.

beats.scene: A narrow highway crowded with carts winds toward a distant town
beats.summary: Politics is but a narrow field; anyone who wants it should follow the market-man along the highway.

beats.scene: One walker crosses a wide empty meadow, no other person in sight
beats.summary: In half an hour he can walk to a place where no man stands from one year's end to another, and politics are not there.

beats.scene: Old philosophers stroll under neat rows of plane trees beside a garden
beats.summary: He asks what would become of us if we walked only in a garden or a public mall, and recalls the philosophers' plane-tree walks.

beats.scene: A walker sits on a log in a wood, eyes shut, lost in thought
beats.summary: It is of no use to direct our steps to the woods if they do not carry us there in spirit.

beats.scene: A sick man on a bed holds a spoon beside a medicine bottle
beats.summary: The walking he means has nothing in common with taking exercise, as the sick take medicine at stated hours.

beats.scene: A man swings heavy dumb-bells in a small room with a clock
beats.summary: He pokes fun at the swinging of dumb-bells or chairs as a way of getting exercise.

beats.scene: A walker sets off down a long path at the start of the day
beats.summary: A true walk is itself the enterprise and adventure of the day.

beats.scene: A spring bubbles from mossy rocks into a green meadow
beats.summary: If you would get exercise, he says, go in search of the springs of life.

beats.scene: A man swings dumb-bells indoors while a meadow brook runs outside
beats.summary: Think of a man swinging dumb-bells for his health while the springs bubble up in far-off pastures unsought by him.

beats.scene: A camel walks slowly across a desert, its face calm and thoughtful
beats.summary: You must walk like a camel, he says, which is said to be the only beast that ruminates when walking.

beats.scene: A servant at a cottage door points toward a hillside and a garden
beats.summary: A traveller asked Wordsworth's servant to see her master's study; she answered that his library was here but his study was out of doors.

beats.scene: A poet with a notebook walks along a lake shore beneath mountains
beats.summary: Wordsworth, the English poet, lived among hills and lakes, walked a great deal and made up many poems out of doors.

beats.scene: A walker with loose hands and eyes on the horizon moves slowly on
beats.summary: To walk like a camel is to let your thoughts chew slowly on the day while your feet keep moving.

beats.scene: A lone walker crosses a field at sunset, boots dusty, face glowing
beats.summary: So a walk is neither medicine nor task but the day's adventure, undertaken by body and mind together.

beats.scene: A walker leaves a farm lane and enters a wide old pasture
beats.summary: He says he walks out into a Nature such as the old prophets and poets walked in.

beats.scene: Four robed figures walk along a green hillside in morning light
beats.summary: He names Menu, Moses, Homer and Chaucer: a legendary lawgiver, a prophet, a Greek poet and an English poet.

beats.scene: An old map of America with a quill resting on the coast
beats.summary: You may name it America, he says, but it is not America; neither Vespucius nor Columbus was its discoverer.

beats.scene: A storyteller reads aloud under a tree to a circle of listeners
beats.summary: There is a truer account of this country in mythology than in any history of America he has seen.

beats.scene: A dusty road crowded with carts, horses and a hurried rider
beats.summary: Roads are made for horses and men of business.

beats.scene: A tavern, a grocery and a depot stand along the same busy road
beats.summary: He is in no hurry to reach any tavern, grocery, livery-stable or depot, the places roads lead to.

beats.scene: A man crosses open land with a stick, a road far behind him
beats.summary: He jokes that he is a good horse to travel, but not from choice a roadster.

beats.scene: A painter at an easel adds a tiny figure to a road
beats.summary: A landscape painter uses the figures of men to mark a road, but he would not use Thoreau's figure that way.

beats.scene: A surveyor's chain stretches across a field beside a boundary stone
beats.summary: As a surveyor he knew the fields, woods and boundary lines around Concord, so he had many ways across country.

beats.scene: A walker steps over a wall, leaving the road hidden behind a hedge
beats.summary: A field has no destination, so the walker who crosses it is simply where he is.

beats.scene: A wide open landscape of fields and woods with no fences
beats.summary: At present, in his neighbourhood, the best part of the land is not private property, so the walker enjoys comparative freedom.

beats.scene: A fenced estate with a locked gate beside a country path
beats.summary: He can imagine a day when the land will be divided into so-called pleasure-grounds, where a few take a narrow and exclusive pleasure.

beats.scene: A tall fence with iron traps along a hedge beside a path
beats.summary: Fences will multiply and man-traps will be invented to confine men to the public road, so that walking on God's earth is called trespassing.

beats.scene: One man stands alone in a huge walled park, looking lonely
beats.summary: To enjoy a thing exclusively is commonly to exclude yourself from the true enjoyment of it.

beats.scene: Walkers cross a bright meadow in morning light before any fence goes up
beats.summary: Let us improve our opportunities, then, before the evil days come.

beats.scene: A signpost at a trail head shows a footpath through open hills
beats.summary: Today some countries, such as Scotland, Sweden and Norway, protect the freedom to walk across much open land.

beats.scene: A river winds through wide meadows toward a green hill in the distance
beats.summary: His own walks led to the Concord River, the Great Meadows and Fair Haven Hill, places he knew in every season.

beats.scene: A circle drawn on a map around a small village, ten miles across
beats.summary: He suggests that the country within about ten miles of home could fill a lifetime of about seventy years.

beats.scene: The same field shown in spring blossom and again under autumn leaves
beats.summary: Even the nearest fields never became quite the same twice, and his journal records the changing dates of flowers and birds.

beats.scene: An open notebook and pencil on a stone wall above fields
beats.summary: To a walker with open eyes, familiar ground is a book to be read again and again.

beats.scene: A walker stands at a fork in a country path, hesitating
beats.summary: What makes it so hard, he asks, to decide which way we will walk?

beats.scene: A magnetised needle on a thread hangs still above a wooden table
beats.summary: He believes there is a subtle magnetism in Nature which, if we unconsciously yield to it, will direct us aright.

beats.scene: A path divides in two; one branch is overgrown with brambles
beats.summary: It is not indifferent which way we walk: there is a right way, but heedlessness and stupidity may lead us wrong.

beats.scene: A trail leaves the edge of a map into unmarked country
beats.summary: We would like to take the walk never yet taken, a perfect symbol of the path we love in our ideal inner world.

beats.scene: A walker holds a pencil over a blank part of a map
beats.summary: Sometimes it is hard to choose because the direction does not yet exist distinctly in our idea.

beats.scene: A compass needle swings to point north on a wooden table
beats.summary: A free needle points north because the Earth acts like a huge magnet, and Thoreau uses it as a picture of an inner pull.

beats.scene: Thoreau stands at his door with a stick, looking over the fields
beats.summary: When he leaves the house, uncertain where to bend his steps, he submits to his instinct to decide for him.

beats.scene: A walker turns slowly on the spot, looking in every direction
beats.summary: Sometimes he turns round and round, irresolute, for a quarter of an hour.

beats.scene: A hat held up to the breeze at the edge of a field
beats.summary: It may seem strange and whimsical to let instinct decide, but the choice, when it comes, is clear and steady.

beats.scene: A pair of boots stands beside a closed gate at dawn
beats.summary: The first act of every walk is a small act of listening, before the first step is taken.

beats.scene: A walker sets off across fields toward a wooded hill in the southwest
beats.summary: He finds that he finally and inevitably settles southwest, toward some particular wood, meadow, deserted pasture or hill.

beats.scene: A compass needle trembles, then settles between west and south-southwest
beats.summary: His needle is slow in settling and varies a few degrees, but it always settles between west and south-southwest.

beats.scene: A walker gazes at green farmland and forest on a western slope
beats.summary: The future lies that way for him, and the earth seems more unexhausted and richer on that side.

beats.scene: A curve drawn on a map opens west, with a small house marked
beats.summary: The outline of his walks would be not a circle but a parabola, opening westward, with his house in the place of the sun.

beats.scene: A comet with a long bright tail arcs across a night sky
beats.summary: Some comets were thought to follow curves that never return, and his walks seem to head away from home in the same way.

beats.scene: Thoreau walks into a glowing western sky with dim land behind him
beats.summary: Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free.

beats.scene: A walker looks east at a grey dawn, away from a faint city
beats.summary: No business leads him west, and he cannot believe he would find wildness and freedom behind the eastern horizon.

beats.scene: A forest stretches to the western horizon beneath a setting sun
beats.summary: He believes the forest in the west stretches unbroken toward the setting sun, with no town or city big enough to disturb him.

beats.scene: A city behind a walker, a wide wilderness spread out ahead
beats.summary: On one side lies the city and on the other the wilderness, and he is ever leaving the city and withdrawing into the wild.

beats.scene: A weathered signpost pointing west with the word Oregon
beats.summary: He thinks this is the tendency of his countrymen: I must walk toward Oregon, and not toward Europe.

beats.scene: Covered wagons cross a wide plain toward a blazing sunset
beats.summary: That way the nation is moving, he says, and mankind progress from east to west.

beats.scene: Settlers load a wagon beside a river at dawn
beats.summary: In his day settlers had crossed the Appalachians and the Mississippi, and wagon trains were setting out for Oregon.

beats.scene: Lodges beside a river under tall trees at dawn, smoke rising
beats.summary: The lands to the west were not empty: Native nations had lived there for thousands of years.

beats.scene: A scholar sits with old books and a map of Greece and Rome
beats.summary: We go eastward to realize history and study the works of art and literature, retracing the steps of the race.

beats.scene: A walker with a lantern heads west at dusk across open hills
beats.summary: We go westward as into the future, with a spirit of enterprise and adventure.

beats.scene: A steamship crosses a wide grey sea toward a low far shore
beats.summary: The Atlantic is a Lethe, he says, in whose passage we have had a chance to forget the Old World and its institutions.

beats.scene: A dark river with a ferryman and a mist-covered far bank
beats.summary: Lethe is the river of forgetting in Greek myth, from which the dead were said to drink.

beats.scene: A tiny ship crosses a vast ocean at sunrise toward a far shore
beats.summary: If we fail this time there is perhaps one more chance, in the Lethe of the Pacific, which he calls three times as wide.

beats.scene: A French botanist on horseback writes notes in a wild forest
beats.summary: The younger Michaux reported that the common question among settlers in the west was, From what part of the world have you come?

beats.scene: A basket of golden fruit rests on a stone wall at sunset
beats.summary: Thoreau offers a Latin saying with a twist: Ex Oriente lux; ex Occidente frux, from the East light, from the West fruit.

beats.scene: A sailing ship heads toward a golden sunset over a calm sea
beats.summary: As he walks west he recalls the old dream of the poets, that a golden land lay where the sun goes down.

beats.scene: Nymphs rest beneath an apple tree hung with golden fruit
beats.summary: The Greeks told of the Hesperides, nymphs who guarded golden apples in a garden at the western edge of the world.

beats.scene: A hero in a lion skin reaches up toward a golden apple
beats.summary: Heracles was sent to fetch some of those golden apples as one of his labours.

beats.scene: A ruined temple on a cliff above a calm sea at dusk
beats.summary: Plato described the island of Atlantis in the west, a rich land that sank; nobody has found evidence that it existed.

beats.scene: Bright flowers cover soft fields under a gentle glowing sky
beats.summary: The Elysian Fields were a blessed country at the edge of the world where heroes were said to rest.

beats.scene: A walker on a hill looks out toward a shining western horizon
beats.summary: Thoreau likes to imagine that the old poets were dreaming of the land in which he lives.

beats.scene: A small three-masted ship sails west under a pale morning sky
beats.summary: Columbus sailed west in 1492 hoping to reach Asia and reached islands of the Americas, new to Europeans.

beats.scene: An Irish bishop in black writes at a plain wooden desk
beats.summary: A line by the Irish bishop George Berkeley says the course of empire moves westward, and Americans often quoted it.

beats.scene: A low sun above a stone wall throws a long shadow eastward
beats.summary: A walker going west in the afternoon has the sun in front of him and his shadow stretching back toward home.

beats.scene: A walker's face lit gold by evening light, eyes half closed
beats.summary: To walk west is to walk into the light, toward the best hours of the day.

beats.scene: A wide night sky over a dark hill thick with bright stars
beats.summary: Thoreau says the heavens of America appear to him infinitely higher, and the stars brighter.

beats.scene: Stars arch over a dark hill and a small lit cabin
beats.summary: He trusts these facts are symbolical of the height to which the philosophy, poetry and religion of its people may one day soar.

beats.scene: A thinker stands in a field and looks up at the night sky
beats.summary: He hopes the immaterial heaven of the mind will appear as much higher and brighter to the American mind.

beats.scene: A hiker breathes deeply on a mountain path in clear air
beats.summary: He believes climate reacts on a person, for there is something in mountain air that feeds the spirit.

beats.scene: A foggy village street at dawn with lamps barely visible
beats.summary: Will we grow in mind as well as body under such influences, or is it unimportant how many foggy days there are in life?

beats.scene: A bright clear sky above a hilltop with a lark rising
beats.summary: He trusts that our thoughts will be clearer, fresher and more ethereal, like our sky.

beats.scene: A wide plain with a thunderstorm approaching over distant mountains
beats.summary: He hopes our understanding will be broad like our plains and our intellect grand like our thunder, rivers, mountains and forests.

beats.scene: A great lake glitters under the sun with no far shore in sight
beats.summary: Last of all he hopes our hearts will match in breadth and depth the inland seas of the continent.

beats.scene: A traveller reaches a hilltop and a wide valley opens below
beats.summary: Else to what end does the world go on, he asks, and why was America discovered?

beats.scene: A telescope stands on a hill under a sky thick with stars
beats.summary: The same stars shine over every land, but a dark place far from lamps shows many more of them.

beats.scene: A wolf's bright eyes shine from the shadows of a dark wood
beats.summary: He asks for a wildness whose glance no civilization can endure.

beats.scene: A kudu antelope with spiral horns stands on a dry open plain

B1B2: Henry David Thoreau spent much of his life on foot, walking the lanes, fields and woods around his home in Concord, Massachusetts. He wrote an essay about those walks, and people around the world still read it today.
Thoreau was born in Concord in 1817, a village of farms and meadows with a slow river running through it. He knew every field and wood around it, and he came back to them again and again.
After he finished his studies at Harvard in 1837, he did not follow the usual path into a well-paid career. He came home to Concord and chose a plain life with plenty of free time.
To pay for his simple life he made pencils in his family's business and worked as a land surveyor. Both jobs left him enough free hours to roam the countryside he was measuring.
Thoreau's older friend and neighbour Ralph Waldo Emerson, a famous writer, encouraged him to write. They often talked and walked together, and their long conversations shaped much of his thinking.
In 1845 Thoreau built a small cabin beside Walden Pond, on land that belonged to Emerson. He lived there for about two years, writing, growing beans and walking in the woods every day.
Thoreau kept a journal for most of his adult life, and it grew into a huge record of what he saw. He noted birds, flowers, weather and the dates when the first leaves appeared.

A few years later he began giving talks about walking and wild nature, some at the Concord Lyceum, where neighbours came to hear lectures. Those talks grew, over several years, into the essay that we are about to follow.
In his last years Thoreau suffered from tuberculosis, a lung disease, but he kept revising his essays for print. He died at home in Concord on 6 May 1862, when he was only 44 years old.
A month later, in June 1862, the Atlantic Monthly printed his essay under the title Walking. It began as a talk, so you can still hear a speaker's voice in it.

Thoreau opens his essay with a clear aim: he wants to speak a word for Nature, and for absolute freedom and wildness. He is not talking about a mild or tidy kind of nature, but about the wide, untamed world.
He compares this freedom with the kind that belongs to society, which he calls merely civil. Laws, votes and good manners give us that kind, and it is real, but he thinks it is a narrow one.
He wants to see a person as an inhabitant, or even a part, of Nature, rather than only as a member of society. In his view, a person is first of all a living creature among many others.
Thoreau knows that this is a one-sided claim, and he says so with a smile. He would rather make an extreme statement that people remember than a careful one that they forget.

There are plenty of champions of civilization already, he points out to his listeners, so he will not add his voice to theirs. The minister, the school committee and every person in the hall will take care of that side of the argument.
Thoreau is not an enemy of towns, schools or churches. He simply wants his listeners to remember that there is a wide world beyond the last fence of the village.
For Thoreau, walking is the plainest way to step outside the rules of society for a while. A walker does not have to break a single law; he only has to leave the road and enter the fields.
He says that in the course of his life he has met only one or two people who understood the art of walking. In other words, plenty of people go for walks, but very few of them truly walk.
Such a person, he says, has a genius for sauntering. Taking a walk is not the same as getting somewhere, and the gift is to enjoy the going.
Then he stops to ask where the odd word saunter comes from. He offers two stories about it, though modern dictionary writers say nobody knows for sure.

In the first story, saunter comes from idle wanderers of the Middle Ages who begged and said they were going to the Holy Land. In French, the Holy Land was called la Sainte Terre, and the story plays on that name.
Whenever such a traveller passed through a village, Thoreau says, children would shout that there goes a Sainte-Terrer. In time that name was bent into saunterer, and the word was born.
Those who never really get to the Holy Land, Thoreau jokes, are mere idlers and vagabonds. But those who do get there are saunterers in the good sense, and that is the kind he means.
The second story says that saunter comes from the French words sans terre, which mean without land. A saunterer, then, is someone with no fixed home, and so is at home everywhere.

Thoreau calls this idea the secret of successful sauntering, and he says it with great confidence. If you feel at home in every field and wood, you never need a destination to feel that you have arrived.
He then says, with a grin, that the person who sits still in a house all the time may be the greatest vagrant of all. A real saunterer, in the good sense, is no more aimless than a river.
A river winds and bends across the land, yet all the while it is looking for the shortest way to the sea. Thoreau says a saunterer is like that: his path may wander, but it is not without purpose.

Of the two stories, Thoreau prefers the first, because it makes every walk sound like an adventure. He says that every walk is a sort of crusade, preached by a Peter the Hermit who lives inside each of us.

The real Peter the Hermit was a preacher of the eleventh century who stirred up crowds to set out for the Holy Land. Thoreau's joke is that a good walk needs just such an inner voice, urging us out of the door.
In this joke the Holy Land is not only a place on a map. It stands for any wild and lovely country that a walker sets out to find, near or far.

Thoreau admits that even the walkers of his own day are rather faint-hearted crusaders, who take on no long, never-ending adventures. Their walks are small, safe and short, and few of them seem to mind.
Our expeditions, he says, are only tours, and by evening we come round again to the old fireside we started from. It is a pleasant habit, but he does not call it a crusade.
Half of every walk, he points out, is just a matter of retracing our own steps. A walk that only returns the way it came has not gone very far in spirit.
He would like us to set out instead in the spirit of undying adventure, never intending to return. Only a walker with that spirit, he feels, is a true crusader.

He imagines setting out so completely that we would send only our embalmed hearts home, as relics for the kingdoms we left behind. It is a strange, grand picture, and it shows how seriously he takes the idea of leaving.

The first condition is a hard one: you must be ready to leave your family and friends and never see them again. He names them one by one, father, mother, brother, sister, wife and child, so the demand sounds like a solemn oath.

The second condition is practical: you must have paid your debts, made your will and settled your affairs, so that you are free. Only then, he says, are you truly ready for a walk, with nothing left to pull you back.
Thoreau is exaggerating, of course, and the joke is part of the lesson. What he means is that a good walker needs a free mind, with no worry or duty tugging at the sleeve.

Thoreau says that he and his walking companion like to imagine themselves knights of a new, or rather an old, order. They are not riders or chevaliers, but Walkers, a class that he trusts is still more ancient and honourable.
The old spirit of chivalry, he thinks, now lives in the Walker rather than the rider. This Walker Errant is a sort of fourth estate, standing outside Church and State and People.

Thoreau feels that he and his companion are almost alone in the neighbourhood in practising this noble art. Most of his neighbours say they would like to walk now and then, as he does, but they cannot.

Money does not solve the problem, he says, because no wealth can buy the leisure, freedom and independence that a walker needs. Those things are the capital of the profession, and they come only as a kind of gift.

It requires a special gift from Heaven, he says, to become a walker, for you must be born into the family of the Walkers. He puts the joke into Latin, Ambulator nascitur, non fit, which means a walker is born, not made.

Thoreau says he cannot keep his health and spirits unless he spends at least four hours a day sauntering in the woods and fields. In practice, he adds, it is commonly more than that, so four hours is only the minimum.
Those hours must be absolutely free from every worldly engagement. No errands, no appointments and no work may follow him into the woods.
He notes that mechanics and shopkeepers stay in their shops all day, sitting with crossed legs, as if legs were made only for sitting. He thinks they deserve credit for putting up with it so long.
He cannot stay in his room for even a single day without gathering some rust. A mind, like a tool left in a damp cellar, soon starts to spoil.
Sometimes he steals out at the eleventh hour, too late to redeem the day. As the shades of night begin to mix with daylight, he feels as if he had committed a sin to be atoned for.
He is astonished at the endurance, and even the moral blindness, of neighbours who stay in shops and offices all day long. They do it for weeks and months, and almost for years together.
Thoreau arranged his whole life to protect these free hours of walking. At Walden he wrote that about six weeks of work in a year could pay all the costs of his simple living.
Sometimes Thoreau walks a mile into the woods with his body but not with his mind. He finds this alarming, because it means that he has gone all that way and has not really arrived.
On his afternoon walk he would gladly forget all his morning work and all his duties to other people. The woods are the one place where he hopes to put down those loads.
But it sometimes happens that he cannot easily shake off the village. The thought of some task runs round in his head, and he is not where his body is.
He says that he is then out of his senses, and that in his walks he would gladly return to them. To be out of one's senses here means to be too busy thinking to see, hear or smell the world.

He puts the question to himself plainly: what business has he in the woods, if he is thinking of something outside the woods? The answer is none, and he is alarmed whenever he catches himself in that state.

Church and State and school, trade and commerce, even politics, the most alarming of them all, take up little space in the landscape. Thoreau is pleased to see how small they look from out in the fields.
Politics, he says, is but a narrow field, and the narrow highway over there leads to it. If you want the political world, follow the great road: follow the market-man and keep his dust in your eyes.
He says he can walk in half an hour to a place where no man stands from one year's end to another. There politics does not exist, for it is only a puff of one man's cigar smoke.

What would become of us, Thoreau asks, if we walked only in a garden or a public mall? He recalls that some sects of philosophers planted groves and walks of plane trees, because they did not go to the woods.
Of course, he adds, it is of no use to direct our steps to the woods if they do not carry us there. A walker who carries his desk along in his head has only moved the desk outdoors.
The walking Thoreau means has nothing in common with exercise as people call it, taken at set hours like medicine by the sick. He does not walk because a doctor or a clock tells him to.
He pokes fun at the swinging of dumb-bells or chairs, a way some people took exercise in his day. To him it seems a sad indoor substitute for the real thing.
A true walk, he says, is itself the enterprise and adventure of the day. It is not a break from real life, or a duty to be ticked off a list; it is the main event.
If you want exercise, Thoreau says, go in search of the springs of life. By this he means the fresh sources of energy, beauty and wonder that bubble up in wild places.
Think of a man swinging dumb-bells for his health, he says, while the springs of life bubble up in far-off pastures unsought by him. The picture is meant to make us smile, and then to make us think.
He also says that you must walk like a camel, which is said to be the only animal that ruminates while walking. To ruminate means to chew food again, and it also means to think things over slowly.

A traveller asked Wordsworth's servant to show him her master's study, and she answered, “Here is his library, but his study is out of doors.” Thoreau repeats the story because it says so much in so few words.
William Wordsworth was an English poet who lived among the hills and lakes of northern England. He was famous for his long walks, and he made up many of his poems as he went along.
To walk like a camel, then, is to let your thoughts chew slowly on the day while your feet keep moving. The best ideas, many people find, arrive at a steady walking pace, not at a desk.
So a walk is neither a medicine nor a task. It is a whole person, body and mind together, setting out on the day's adventure.
When Thoreau leaves the house, he does not want to walk in a tidy, tamed countryside. He wants to walk out into a Nature such as the old prophets and poets walked in.
He names four of them: Menu, Moses, Homer and Chaucer. They were a legendary lawgiver of India, the prophet Moses, a Greek poet and an English poet of the Middle Ages.
You may call that Nature America, he says, but it is not America. Neither Americus Vespucius, nor Columbus, nor the other explorers were its discoverers, for it is older than any of their names.

Thoreau says that there is a truer account of this wild country in mythology than in any history of America that he has seen. Old stories, he feels, remember what mattered about the land, while history books often record only who owned it and who fought for it.
Roads, he says, are made for horses and men of business, who want to get somewhere in a hurry. That is why he does not use them very much.
He is not in a hurry to reach any tavern, grocery, livery-stable or depot, the places to which roads lead. A man with no wish to arrive anywhere in particular has little use for a road.
He jokes that he is a good horse to travel, but not from choice a roadster. A roadster is a horse used on the road, and he would rather run free across country.
He adds that a landscape painter often uses the figure of a man to mark a road in his picture. The painter, he says, would not make that use of Thoreau's figure.

Thoreau earned part of his living as a land surveyor, so he knew the fields, woods and boundary lines around Concord very well. That knowledge gave him many ways to cross the country without ever setting foot on the road.
A field has no tavern at the end of it, and it asks nothing of the person who crosses it. The walker in a field is not on his way to anything; he is simply where he is.
Thoreau notes that in his own neighbourhood the best part of the land is not private property. The landscape is not owned, and so the walker enjoys a comparative freedom.

But he can imagine a day when it will be divided into so-called pleasure-grounds, where a few people will take a narrow and exclusive pleasure. The word pleasure sounds generous, but the grounds will be closed to everyone else.

Fences will be multiplied, he warns, and man-traps and other engines invented to confine men to the public road. Walking over the surface of God's earth may even be called trespassing on some gentleman's grounds.
To enjoy a thing exclusively, he says, is commonly to exclude yourself from the true enjoyment of it. A park shut off for one owner, he implies, may give less joy than a field open to all.
Let us improve our opportunities, then, he says, before the evil days come. The message is urgent but cheerful: walk freely now, while the fields are still open.
In some countries today the law protects this kind of freedom to walk. In Scotland, Sweden and Norway, for example, people may walk across much open country if they follow simple rules.
Thoreau's own walks led him to the Concord River, the Great Meadows and Fair Haven Hill, places he knew in every season. Some of that countryside is still open to walkers today.

He believes that the country within about ten miles of his home, the distance of an afternoon's walk, could fill a lifetime of walks. A lifetime of about seventy years, he suggests, would still not be long enough to use it up.
Even the nearest fields, he found, never became quite the same twice. In his journal he noted the dates when flowers opened and birds returned, and those dates were different every year.
A walker with open eyes, Thoreau suggests, is never short of new places, even in his own back yard. The countryside is a book that can be read again and again.
Thoreau asks a question that every walker knows: what makes it so hard, sometimes, to decide where we will walk? At the door, with the whole countryside before us, we often stand and hesitate.
His answer is a hopeful one: he believes there is a subtle magnetism in Nature that can guide us. If we yield to it without thinking, it will direct us aright.
It is not indifferent to us, he says, which way we walk. There is a right way, but through heedlessness and stupidity we are very liable to take the wrong one.
We would like to take the walk that we have never yet taken, he says, through this real world. Such a walk would be a perfect symbol of the path we love to follow in our inner, ideal world.
Sometimes, no doubt, we find it hard to choose a direction. The reason, he suggests, is that the path does not yet exist clearly in our own idea.
A compass needle is a good picture for this inner pull. It points north because the Earth itself acts like a huge magnet, and a needle that is free to turn will find north.
When Thoreau goes out of the house for a walk, he often does not yet know where he will go. He submits to his instinct to decide for him, and waits to feel which way he is drawn.
Sometimes he turns round and round, irresolute, for a quarter of an hour. Anyone who has stood in a doorway, unable to choose a path, will recognise the feeling.
It may seem strange and whimsical, he admits, to let instinct decide. But he finds that the choice, once it comes, is a clear and steady one, and he trusts it.
So the first act of every walk, for Thoreau, is a small act of listening. Before the first step, he waits to feel where the day wants him to go.
When Thoreau lets his instinct decide, he finds that he finally and inevitably settles on the southwest. He heads toward some particular wood, meadow, deserted pasture or hill in that direction.
His needle, as he calls it, is slow in settling. It varies a few degrees and does not always point due southwest, but it always settles somewhere between west and south-southwest.
The future lies that way, he feels, and the earth on that side seems richer and less worn out. To him it seems unexhausted, as though it still had something new to give.
He says that the outline of his walks would not be a circle but a parabola, like the path of a comet. It would open toward the west, and his house would stand where the sun stands.
Some comets, people once thought, follow curves that never return. Thoreau likes the picture, because his walks also seem to head away from home and not look back.
He puts it in a single line: eastward I go only by force, but westward I go free. A walk to the west feels like his own choice, while a walk to the east feels like a duty.
No business leads him west, which is part of its charm. It is hard for him to believe that he would find fair landscapes, or enough wildness and freedom, behind the eastern horizon.
He believes that the forest he sees on the western horizon stretches without a break toward the setting sun. There are no towns or cities in it large enough, he says, to disturb him.
Wherever he lives, he says, the city lies on one side and the wilderness on the other. He is always leaving the city more and more, and withdrawing into the wilderness.
He would not stress this if he did not think that most of his countrymen feel the same pull. I must walk toward Oregon, he declares, and not toward Europe.
That way the nation is moving, Thoreau says, and he adds that mankind progress from east to west. It is a sweeping claim, and he states it as plainly as a weather report.
In his day there was plenty of evidence for the claim. Settlers had crossed the Appalachian mountains and the Mississippi River, and by 1843 wagon trains were setting out for Oregon.
But the lands to the west were not empty. Native nations had lived there for thousands of years, and the westward movement that Thoreau praises took the land from many of them.
He says that we go east to study history, art and literature, retracing the steps of the human race. Going east, for him, means looking back at what people have already done.
We go westward, on the other hand, as into the future, with a spirit of enterprise and adventure. West is where a person goes to make something new, not to study something old.

The Atlantic, Thoreau says, is a Lethe, and in passing over it we have had a chance to forget the Old World and its institutions. Many Americans of his day were, after all, people or the children of people who had crossed it to start again.
Lethe is the river of forgetting in Greek myth, and Thoreau uses its name as a picture. The dead were said to drink its waters, so that they would forget their earlier lives.

If we fail this time, he says, there is perhaps one more chance for humankind before it reaches the banks of the Styx. That chance is in the Lethe of the Pacific, which he says is three times as wide.
The younger Michaux, a French botanist, travelled west of the Alleghanies in 1802. He reported that the common question among the new settlers was, “From what part of the world have you come?”

Thoreau plays on an old Latin saying and turns it into a joke: Ex Oriente lux; ex Occidente FRUX. It means that light comes from the East, but the fruit of that light, in his opinion, comes from the West.
As he walks west, Thoreau remembers an old dream of the poets. They imagined that somewhere beyond the setting sun, across the ocean, there lay a golden land of ease and plenty.

The Greeks told of the Hesperides, nymphs who guarded a tree of golden apples in a garden at the western edge of the world. Their name is linked to a Greek word for evening, the time when the sun sets.
One of the hero Heracles's famous labours was to fetch some of those golden apples. The story shows how the Greeks pictured the far west as a place of danger, beauty and treasure.

The philosopher Plato described another western land, the island of Atlantis, a rich and powerful place that sank beneath the sea. Nobody has ever found evidence that it existed, and most scholars treat it as a story.
The Greek poets also pictured the Elysian Fields, a blessed country at the edge of the world where heroes were said to rest. Like the Hesperides, it was often imagined in the far west.

Thoreau likes to imagine that these old poets were dreaming of the land in which he lives. A country of wide forests, fresh soil and room to grow could, he thinks, be the golden island they had in mind.

Columbus, too, looked to the west, sailing out across the Atlantic in 1492 in search of a new route to Asia. Instead he reached islands of the Americas, which were new to Europeans, and a new age began.
A line by the Irish bishop George Berkeley, written about 1726, says that empire moves westward. Many Americans of Thoreau's day knew it well, and it matched the way they pictured their own future.
A walker who goes west in the afternoon has the setting sun in front of him. His shadow stretches out behind him toward home, and it grows longer as the sun sinks.

So for Thoreau, walking west means walking into the light, toward the best hours of the day. The habit has a practical side, since an afternoon walker who heads west keeps the evening glow before his eyes.
Thoreau now makes a cheerful claim about the sky above his own country. The heavens of America, he says, appear to him infinitely higher, and the stars brighter.
He trusts that these facts are symbolical of the height to which the philosophy, poetry and religion of its people may one day soar. The sky, in other words, is a sign of what the mind can reach.
One day, he hopes, the heaven of the mind will seem as high and as bright as the sky above it. He means the inner sky of thought, where ideas shine like stars.
He believes that climate reacts on a person, because there is something in mountain air that feeds the spirit and inspires. Anyone who has climbed a hill on a clear morning may agree.
Will a person grow to greater perfection in mind as well as body under such influences? Or is it unimportant how many foggy days there are in his life, after all?

He trusts that Americans will be more imaginative, and that their thoughts will be clearer, fresher and more ethereal, like their sky. Ethereal means light and airy, as if made of the same stuff as the air.

He hopes that their understanding will be more comprehensive and broader, like their plains. Their minds, he says, will be on a grander scale, like their thunder and lightning, their rivers, mountains and forests.

Last of all, he hopes that our hearts will correspond in breadth and depth and grandeur to our inland seas. The inland seas are the Great Lakes, so vast that a person on one shore cannot see across, and their storms have wrecked many ships.
He then asks two big questions: else to what end does the world go on, and why was America discovered? If the new world does not bring a new height of mind, he asks, what was the point of finding it?

Of course, the same stars shine over every land, and Thoreau's claim is a poet's joke as much as a fact. Stars do look brighter, though, from a dark place far from lamps and cities, and that is a pleasure any walker can try.
Thoreau now asks for something much stronger than a pleasant park or a tidy garden. Give me a wildness, he says, whose glance no civilization can endure.
He adds, with a grin, that he wants a wildness as strong as the marrow of an African antelope, eaten raw. His word for the animal was koodoo, and the picture is meant to shock a polite audience.
Hope and the future for him are not in lawns and cultivated fields, nor in towns and cities. They are, he says, in the impervious and quaking swamps, which no plough can enter.
When he once thought of buying a farm, he found he was attracted only by a few rods of bog in one corner. That wet corner, he says, was the jewel which dazzled him.

He says he draws more of his subsistence from the swamps around his native town than from the cultivated gardens of the village. He means more than food: the gardens give vegetables, and the swamps give him something wilder to feed on.

There are no richer flower beds in his eyes than the dense beds of dwarf andromeda that cover the soft places on the earth's surface. The plant is a low shrub of bogs with small white bell-shaped flowers in spring.
Botany, he says, can go no further than telling him the names of the shrubs that grow there. They are the high blueberry, azalea and rhodora, all standing in quaking moss.
The moss in a swamp is called sphagnum, and it holds huge amounts of water, like a sponge. That is why the ground quakes underfoot, and why a careless walker may sink in up to the knee.
He enters a swamp as a sacred place, like the innermost room of a temple. There, he says, is the strength, the marrow of Nature.
The wild wood covers the virgin soil, he writes, and the same soil is good for men and for trees. The wood and the person, he means, feed from the same ground.
A man's health, Thoreau says, requires as many acres of meadow in his view as his farm requires loads of muck. Muck is farm manure, which farmers spread on the soil to make crops grow.
A wide view of untamed meadow is, for him, a kind of food for the eyes and the spirit. There are the strong meats, he says, on which a person feeds.

A town is saved, Thoreau says, not more by the righteous men in it than by the woods and swamps that surround it. It is a surprising thing to say at a time when many people saw woods mainly as timber and future farmland.

A township with one primitive forest waving above and another rotting below, he says, can raise poets and philosophers as well as corn and potatoes. The living trees and the fallen ones together make the soil.
In such soil, he says, grew Homer and Confucius and the rest. Out of such a wilderness comes the Reformer eating locusts and wild honey.

Homer was the Greek poet of the Iliad, and Confucius was a Chinese teacher who lived about twenty-five centuries ago. The Reformer eating locusts and wild honey is John the Baptist, who preached in the desert.
Life consists with wildness, Thoreau says: the most alive is the wildest. A wild thing is not yet subdued to man, and its presence refreshes him.
In another essay he asked why the nation should not keep wild preserves, where the bear and the panther could still live. They should not, he said, be civilized off the face of the earth.

A person who pressed forward without rest and asked a great deal of life would always find himself in a new country. He would be surrounded by the raw material of life, climbing over the fallen trunks of old forest trees.

Everything he has said leads to one famous line: in Wildness is the preservation of the World. Many readers have taken those words as a motto, and they are often quoted in speeches about protecting wild land.

The civilized nations, Thoreau says, Greece, Rome and England, have been sustained by the primitive forests which anciently rotted where they stand. Their farms, cities and libraries all rest on the soil that those forests made.
Such nations survive, he says, only while the soil is not exhausted. He warns that little can be expected of a nation when its soil is worn out and it must make manure of its fathers' bones.
The founders of every state that has risen to eminence, he says, have drawn their nourishment and vigour from a similar wild source. A strong people, in his view, begins on rough ground.
According to the Roman legend, the twin founders of Rome, Romulus and Remus, were suckled by a she-wolf. Thoreau turns the legend into a lesson about nations that lose touch with wild strength.

The children of the Empire, he says, were not suckled by the wolf, so they were displaced by the children of the northern forests. Historians give many reasons for the fall of Rome, but Thoreau's picture is a vivid one.
In literature, too, he says, it is only the wild that attracts us. Dulness, he adds, is but another name for tameness, and a tame book is soon forgotten.
It is the uncivilized, free and wild thinking in Hamlet and the Iliad, in all the Scriptures and mythologies, that delights us. Such thinking, he says, is not learned in the schools.

A wild duck is swifter and more beautiful than a tame one, Thoreau says, and wild thought is the same. He means the mallard, the wild ancestor of most ducks on farms, which wings its way over the marshes in falling dew.
A truly good book, he says, is as natural and unexpectedly perfect as a wild flower found on a prairie or in a jungle. Its beauty seems almost unaccountable, as though it had grown by itself.
Genius, he says, is a light that makes the darkness visible, like the flash of lightning. It is not a taper lighted at the hearth-stone of the race, which grows pale in the light of common day.

In Thoreau's opinion, English literature from the minstrels to the Lake Poets, even Shakespeare included, has no truly fresh and wild strain. He finds it tame and civilized, a literature that mostly reflects Greece and Rome.
England's wilderness, he says, is a green wood, and its wild man is a Robin Hood. The outlaw of the old ballads is lively and likeable, but he is a long way from the real forest.
There is plenty of genial love of Nature in these writers, he allows, but not so much of Nature herself. They like a pleasant view from a window; he wants the weather, the mud and the wind.

Alexander von Humboldt was a famous German naturalist, and Thoreau says that the science of Humboldt is one thing and poetry another. Despite all the discoveries of science, he says, the poet today has no advantage over Homer.
Where, he asks, is the literature that gives expression to Nature? He would be a poet who could make the winds and streams speak for him.

Such a poet would nail words to their primitive senses, as farmers drive down stakes in the spring, when the frost has heaved them up. Frost lifts stakes out of the soil, and in the same way words drift away from their first meanings.

He would also derive his words afresh each time he used them, transplanting them into his writing with earth still clinging to their roots. A word taken that way, like a wild plant carried carefully on a spade, keeps its life.

His words would be so true and fresh and natural that they would seem to expand like buds at the approach of spring. This would happen even though they lay half smothered between two musty leaves in a library.
They would bloom and bear fruit there, after their kind, every year, for the faithful reader who reads in sympathy with surrounding Nature. A book of that sort never goes out of season.
Thoreau tried hard to write in just this way, and many readers think he succeeded. His journal is full of sentences written close to the moment of seeing, with a little of the soil still on them.
Thoreau closes his essay with a memory of a late afternoon in November. It had been a cold, grey day, and the sky hung low over the fields.
He was walking across a meadow at the edge of a wood when the sun broke through. It shone low in the sky, and the grey afternoon changed at once.
The softest, brightest light fell on the dry grass, on the stems of the trees and on the leaves of the shrub oaks. Everything it touched seemed to glow from within, like a lamp behind a paper shade.
Every tree and shrub threw a long shadow across the meadow. The land lay quiet, as if it too were pausing to look at the light.
The air was so warm and calm that nothing seemed to be missing. It felt to him that nothing was wanting to make a paradise of that meadow.
In New England in late November the sun sets before half past four, so this kind of light is brief. A walker has only a short time to enjoy it before the cold and the dark return.
Such an evening, he implies, comes without notice and is seen only by someone who is out of doors and awake to it. The people at their desks and counters will never know that it happened.
So, he ends, we saunter toward the Holy Land. The goal is not a place to stop but a direction to keep walking.
He hopes that one day the sun will shine more brightly than ever before. It may even shine into our minds and hearts, as it shone into that meadow.
That light, he says, will light up our whole lives with a great awakening light. It will be as warm and serene and golden as on a bank-side in autumn.
Thoreau is buried in Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in Concord, on a wooded ridge near his friends Emerson and Hawthorne. His own headstone is small and carries a single word, his first name.
His book Walden was not widely read when it first appeared in 1854, but over time it became one of the best-loved books in America. Walking, printed after his death, is often read beside it.
Later nature writers shared his love of wild places. John Muir, who founded the Sierra Club in 1892, wrote that wildness is a necessity.
In 1964 the United States passed the Wilderness Act, a law that protects large areas of wild land. It speaks of land where nature is left free, and it carries an echo of Thoreau's old argument.
Thoreau's lesson is that you do not need a vast wilderness to feel the wild. A field, a stream or a city park may be enough, if you bring your full attention to it.
Try a short saunter of your own, with no destination and no hurry. Walk slowly, leave your errands and worries behind, and let your senses do the work.
Carry a small notebook, as he did, and write down what you notice: the first flower, the sky, a bird's song. Over a year, those small notes will become a record of your own place.

Walking is also widely recommended today as a gentle way to stay active. Many health organizations suggest that most adults aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, and a brisk walk counts toward that.

Thoreau was a writer and not a doctor, and his remarks about health are his own opinions. If you have a health condition or any doubt about exercise, ask a doctor or another professional before you begin.
This book retells Thoreau's essay and gives general information, and it is not medical advice. Walk gently, within your own limits, and enjoy every step.
C1C2: Henry David Thoreau spent a large part of his life on foot, wandering the lanes, fields and wooded hills that surround Concord, Massachusetts, the village where he was born. He wrote an essay about those wanderings, called simply Walking, and it is still read by people who have never set foot in Concord. Come with him now, one short step at a time, and see why a man who went nowhere in particular believed that his daily walk was the real enterprise of the day.

Concord, in Thoreau's day, was a farming village of perhaps two thousand people, set among meadows and orchards beside a slow river, with woods rising on every side. He was born there in 1817, and apart from a few journeys he spent nearly his whole life within reach of its boundaries. Few writers have known one small place so thoroughly, or found so much in it.

After graduating from Harvard in 1837, Thoreau declined the respectable careers that were open to a college man and came home to Concord. He taught school for a while, worked with his hands, and refused to be hurried into a life that would have left him no time to think. Some of his neighbours found him puzzling, and he did not much mind, for he had work of his own to do in the fields and woods.

He earned his bread in modest ways: he helped in his family's pencil-making business, surveyed land for farmers, and took odd jobs whenever he needed money. These trades suited him because the work was brief and the free hours were many. Better still, surveying sent him tramping through meadows and woodlots that most people never saw.

His closest friend and neighbour was Ralph Waldo Emerson, an older and already famous writer, who admired his talent and urged him to put his thoughts on paper. The two men walked and talked together for years, and Emerson's library and conversation helped to shape the younger man's ideas. Yet Thoreau was never a mere follower, and he went his own way, often in directions that his famous friend found hard to follow.

In the summer of 1845 Thoreau built himself a small cabin beside Walden Pond, a short walk from Concord, on land that belonged to Emerson. He stayed for about two years, writing, growing beans and walking the woods every day, and later turned the experience into his famous book Walden. It was an experiment in living simply, and its lessons about time and attention lie just beneath the surface of his essay on walking.

All his life Thoreau kept a journal, and by the end it had grown into a vast record of the countryside around him. He set down the first appearance of a flower, the arrival of a bird, the colour of the leaves and the warmth of a certain afternoon, often with the date. Such patient attention is the root of his walking, for a man who looks that closely never walks the same road twice.

A few years after leaving the pond, Thoreau began to give talks on walking and wild nature, some of them at the Concord Lyceum, a hall where townspeople gathered to hear lectures. He revised and expanded the material many times, trying out phrases on his audiences and cutting whatever fell flat. By the time it reached its final form, it had the rhythm of a speaker who knows how to make a crowd smile before he asks it to think.

In his last years Thoreau suffered from tuberculosis, a serious lung disease that was common and often fatal in that age, yet he went on revising his essays for the press. He died at home in Concord on 6 May 1862, at the age of only forty-four, with his family around him. His sister Sophia afterward helped to look after his papers, so that the essays he had been revising could still reach the public.

A month later, in June 1862, the Atlantic Monthly printed the essay under the plain title Walking, so that for many readers it arrived like a message from a man who had just left the room. It began its life as a talk, and you can still hear the speaker's voice in its jokes, its sudden quotations and its bold claims. Let us follow it now, in his order, from the first line to the last.

Thoreau begins his essay with a bold announcement: he wishes to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness, as against the freedom and culture that are merely civil. He does not mean a tamed and tidy nature, with paths and benches, but the wide, untouched world that goes on without us. It is an odd subject for a lecture delivered in a lamp-lit hall, and he knows it very well.

By civil freedom he means the kind that a good society can give: the protection of laws, the right to vote, the pleasure of polite company. It is real and valuable, but Thoreau finds it narrow, a freedom that lives inside walls. Beyond those walls lies a larger liberty, and the whole essay is an attempt to point toward it.

He asks us to picture a human being differently: not first as a citizen, a customer or a church member, but as an inhabitant of Nature, one living thing among countless others. Most writers, he implies, begin with society and treat the wild as a mere backdrop. Thoreau turns the picture around, so that the village becomes a small clearing in a very large forest.

Thoreau admits that he wants to make an extreme statement, if that is the only way to make an emphatic one. A mild claim slips out of the mind before the audience has reached the door, whereas a startling one stays. He is a teacher who knows the value of surprise, and he uses it without apology.

There are enough champions of civilization already, he says with a twinkle: the minister, the school committee and every member of his audience will take care of that. His own part is to speak for the other side, the side that has few friends in a lecture hall. A fair debate, after all, needs somebody willing to stand up and argue for the forest.

None of this makes Thoreau an enemy of towns, schools or churches, and he lived beside all three for his whole life. He simply wants his listeners to remember that a larger world lies beyond the last fence of the village. A person who forgets that world, he suggests, has forgotten half of what it means to be alive.

For Thoreau, walking is the simplest way to step outside the rules of society for an afternoon. A walker does not have to break a single law, argue with a single neighbour or give up a single comfort of home. He has only to leave the road, climb a wall and let the fields take him in.

In the whole course of his life, Thoreau declares, he has encountered scarcely one or two people who truly understood the art of walking, which is the art of taking a walk well. That is a startling claim from a man whose neighbours trudged to church, to market and to work every day. His point is that travelling from one place to another is a mere necessity, whereas walking for its own sake is a discipline and an art.

Such a person, he says, has a genius for sauntering: a gift for moving slowly through the world with an open mind and no appointment to keep. The gift has little to do with strength, speed or distance, and everything to do with attention. A saunterer may cover only a mile in an afternoon and still see more than a traveller who covers twenty.

Then, with a sudden turn, he stops to ask where the odd word saunter comes from, and he offers two stories about it. Both are pleasing, though today's dictionary makers admit that nobody knows the true origin for certain. The reader is free to enjoy them as Thoreau did, as small fables about the word's journey.

Thoreau offers two explanations of the word saunter, and he plainly enjoys both of them. In the first, it comes from idle wanderers of the Middle Ages, who roamed the country begging for charity and claiming to be bound for the Holy Land, which the French called Sainte Terre. Whether true or not, it is a tale with a smile in it, and he tells it with the straight face of a man who knows how funny it is.

As such a traveller passed through a village, Thoreau says, the children would cry out that there went a Sainte-Terrer, a Holy-Lander. Said again and again by children at play, the name could easily wear down into saunterer. A word that began as a jeer, he suggests, became the name of an art.

Those who never actually reach the Holy Land in their walks, Thoreau jokes, are mere idlers and vagabonds, whatever they pretend. But those who do go there are saunterers in the good sense, and that is the sense he intends for the word. In his mouth it becomes a compliment, the highest one he can pay to a person on foot.

The second story is shorter, and to many readers it is more satisfying, because it fits the walker's way of life. It says that saunter comes from the French sans terre, meaning without land, so that a saunterer is a person with no particular home. By this account, the saunterer belongs to the whole countryside at once, as a bird or a cloud belongs to the sky.

Having no particular home, Thoreau reasons, means being equally at home everywhere, and that is the secret of successful sauntering. A person who is at home in every meadow and every wood has no need to hurry back to any one house. Wherever the walker stands, he has arrived, and the road ahead holds no more promise than the ground beneath his feet.

He adds, with a grin, that the man who sits still in his house all the time may be the greatest vagrant of all. The saunterer, in the good sense, is no more a vagrant than the meandering river, which is all the while earnestly seeking the shortest course to the sea. A path may curve and double back, he implies, and still be going somewhere.

Look at a river from above and you will see it loop and wander across the land, taking a hundred bends where a ruler would draw one line. Yet at every moment the water is going downhill, and every bend is part of its journey to the sea. Thoreau wants us to see the saunterer in that light, as a person whose wandering is a kind of faithfulness.

Of the two stories, Thoreau prefers the first, because it turns an ordinary stroll into an expedition. Every walk, he says, is a sort of crusade, preached to us by some Peter the Hermit within, who urges us to go forth and win back the Holy Land. The idea is playful, but it carries a serious thought: a walk should feel like a quest, not a chore.

The real Peter the Hermit was a wandering preacher of the eleventh century, whose fiery sermons helped to rouse thousands of ordinary people to set out for the Holy Land in the First Crusade. Thoreau borrows him as a comic figure, the voice inside us that cries out when we sit too long at a desk. Without such a voice, he implies, most of us would never find the door.

For Thoreau, then, the Holy Land is not only a place on the map of the Middle East. It is whatever wild and beautiful country a walker sets out to find, and it may lie a hundred miles away or just over the nearest hill. What matters is the spirit of the setting out, the sense that something worth finding is waiting.

Thoreau confesses that even the keenest walkers of his day are rather faint-hearted crusaders, who set out on no persevering, never-ending enterprise. Their excursions are brief and comfortable, planned so that nothing is risked and nothing is left behind. A true crusade, he suggests, would ask for more courage than an afternoon stroll ever requires.

Our expeditions, he complains, are mere tours, and by evening we come round again to the old hearth-side from which we set out. We carry our comforts with us in spirit, and we are careful to be home before dark, with the lamp lit and the kettle on. There is nothing wrong with such a habit, but it is not the habit of a person who has really set out.

Half the walk, Thoreau observes, is only a matter of retracing our steps, as if the best part of the journey were the return.
