A path that circles back to its starting point offers the walker a pleasant outing, but it seldom offers him the unknown. He would like each walk to lead a little further into country that he has never seen.

He wishes that we would go forth in the spirit of undying adventure, never intending to return, ready to meet whatever the road might bring. Such a walker would give himself to the journey as completely as the old crusaders gave themselves to theirs. The difference, of course, is that his holy land is a wood or a meadow, and his only enemy is the clock.

If we truly meant it, he says, we should be prepared to send back our embalmed hearts only as relics to our desolate kingdoms. The picture is deliberately extravagant and recalls an old custom of sending home the hearts of knights who died far away. Thoreau uses it to shake us out of our caution and to ask how much of ourselves we are willing to carry out of the door.

The first condition is a hard one, and he states it without softening: you must be ready to leave father and mother, brother and sister, wife and child and friends, and never see them again. He names them one by one, so that the demand falls on the ear like a solemn vow. No one is expected to obey it to the letter, but the list shows how much a true walker must be willing to let go.

The second condition is more practical, and it is the one that would trouble most of us: you must have paid your debts, made your will and settled all your affairs. Only if you are, in his words, a free man, with nothing left unfinished behind you, are you ready for a walk. A mind weighed down by unpaid bills, Thoreau implies, will carry them into the meadow and never see the flowers.

These demands are half a joke, and Thoreau delivers them with a straight face, as he often does. Beneath the exaggeration lies a serious point: a good walk needs a free mind, and a mind that is still at the office will not notice the birds. He is not asking anyone to abandon a family, only to be present when walking, as fully as a person can be.

To come down to his own experience, he says, he and his walking companion take pleasure in fancying themselves knights of a new, or rather an old, order. They are not riders or chevaliers, but Walkers, a still more ancient and honourable class, as he trusts. The joke is gentle and the pride is real, since walking is the oldest way of travelling that human beings know.

The chivalric spirit that once belonged to the horseman, he thinks, seems now to live in the walker instead, a knight on foot who goes wherever the adventure leads. He calls this figure the Walker Errant, and describes him as a sort of fourth estate, outside of Church and State and People. It is a lovely joke, and it makes a serious point: the walker answers to the open country before he answers to any institution.

Thoreau feels that he and his walking companion are almost alone in the neighbourhood in practising this noble art. Most of his townsmen, to hear them talk, would gladly walk now and then, as he does, but somehow they never can. The complaint is gently made, yet it carries a sting, because he knows how seldom the wish turns into an actual walk.

The difficulty, he explains, is not a shortage of money, for no wealth can buy the leisure, freedom and independence that are the capital in this profession. A rich man who is chained to his business is as poor in free hours as the humblest clerk. The walker's wealth is measured in unclaimed afternoons, and that kind of fortune cannot be purchased at any price.

Such leisure comes only by the grace of God, Thoreau says, and it requires a direct dispensation from Heaven to become a walker. You must be born into the family of the Walkers, and he settles the matter with a flourish of schoolroom Latin: Ambulator nascitur, non fit, a walker is born and not made. It is a joke at his own expense, since it makes a gift of what he has in fact worked hard to arrange.

By his own account, Thoreau cannot preserve his health and spirits unless he spends at least four hours a day, and commonly a good deal more, sauntering through the woods and over the hills and fields. These hours are no luxury, in his view, but the foundation of every other kind of work. A man who tries to write, think or even feel on an empty stock of fresh air, he implies, soon runs short of all three.

He insists that the hours must be absolutely free from all worldly engagements, and he means the word absolutely. A walk with half an eye on the clock, or with an errand waiting at the far end, is only a short journey in disguise. The saunterer's afternoon belongs to nobody but himself, the open sky and the fields that he crosses.

He observes that the mechanics and shopkeepers sit in their shops not only all morning but all afternoon too, with crossed legs, as if legs were made to sit upon rather than to walk upon. Thoreau, with his dry humour, thinks they deserve some credit for putting up with it for so long. He cannot imagine bearing such a life himself, for even one day indoors leaves him feeling stale and stiff.

Thoreau confesses that he cannot stay in his room for a single day without acquiring some rust, like an unused tool left to the damp. His thoughts grow slow and heavy, his spirits sink, and the whole world seems smaller than it is. A walk, by contrast, scrapes the rust away and leaves the mind bright and ready.

Sometimes, he says, he has stolen out at the eleventh hour, too late to redeem the day, when the shades of night were already mixing with the daylight. On such evenings he has felt as if he had committed some sin that needed to be atoned for. It is the guilt of a man who has wasted a precious gift, and he describes it with more humour than shame.

What astonishes him most is the power of endurance, to say nothing of the moral insensibility, of those neighbours who confine themselves to shops and offices the whole day, for weeks and months and even years together. He is not unkind about it, for most of them, no doubt, have families to feed and bills to pay. But he cannot help wondering what they have given up, and whether they even notice that it is gone.

Thoreau arranged his whole life, down to the smallest expense, so as to protect these free hours of walking. At Walden he reckoned that by working about six weeks in a year he could meet all the costs of his simple living, which left the rest of the year for study, writing and the fields. Few of us could copy his bargain exactly, but the lesson remains: time to walk is not found by accident, and it must be defended.

Sometimes, Thoreau confesses, he walks a mile into the woods in body without ever getting there in spirit. He has covered the ground and passed the trees, yet his mind is elsewhere, still turning over the business of the morning. The discovery alarms him, for it means that the walk, which he values above almost everything, has been quietly wasted.

In his afternoon walk he would gladly forget all his morning occupations and all his obligations to society. The hours of the day have a way of piling up like sediment, and he wants to wash his mind clear of them before the evening. The woods, to him, are a place of rinsing as well as a place of beauty.

But it sometimes happens that he cannot easily shake off the village, however far he may have walked from its last house. The thought of some piece of work runs in his head, and he is not where his body is; as he puts it, he is out of his senses. It is a small comedy of the mind, and nearly everyone who has tried to relax on a holiday knows it well.

In his walks, he says, he would gladly return to his senses: he would look, listen and breathe with the whole of himself. The senses are the doors by which the world comes in, and they stay shut when the mind is busy with its accounts. He wants them thrown wide open, like the windows of a house on the first warm day of spring.

What business has he in the woods, he asks himself bluntly, if he is thinking of something outside the woods? The question has no comfortable answer, and he does not try to invent one. A walker who is not truly present, he seems to say, has no business there at all.

Church and State and school, trade and commerce, manufactures and farming, even politics, the most alarming of them all, occupy very little space in the landscape, and Thoreau is pleased to see it. From a hilltop the great institutions of the age look no larger than a few roofs and a thread of road. The proportions of the world, it seems, are truer when seen from a field than from a desk.

Politics, he adds, is only a narrow field, and the still narrower highway over yonder leads to it. If a traveller wants the political world, Thoreau will gladly point the way: follow the market-man, keep his dust in your eyes, and the road will lead you straight to it. Politics, after all, has its place merely, and it does not fill all of space.

In one half-hour, Thoreau says, he can walk off to some part of the earth's surface where a man does not stand from one year's end to another. In such a place there is, consequently, no politics, for it is no more than the cigar smoke of one man. It is a delightful way of cutting the greatest worries down to size, and the fields are the proof.

What would become of us, Thoreau asks, if we walked only in a garden or a public mall? Even some sects of philosophers, he recalls, felt the need to import the woods to themselves, and planted groves and walks of plane trees where they could stroll in the open air. They did so because they did not go to the woods, and an imitation, however handsome, is a poor substitute for the thing itself.

Of course, he adds, it is of no use to direct our steps to the woods if they do not carry us there in spirit. A walker who brings his desk along in his head has only moved his desk outdoors, and the trees will keep their secrets from him. The cure, Thoreau implies, is not a better path or a longer walk but a quieter and more attentive mind.

The walking of which Thoreau speaks has nothing in common with what people call taking exercise, as the sick take medicine at stated hours. He will not hear of a walk that is measured out in doses, with so many minutes to be got through for the good of the heart. To him, a walk of that kind has already lost the thing that makes it worth taking.

He pokes fun at the swinging of dumb-bells or chairs, a way some people took their exercise in his day, shut up in a room. Such labour is all effort and no arrival; the muscles move, but nothing is seen and nothing is found. It is a sad indoor imitation of the real thing, and Thoreau cannot take it seriously.

A true walk, he says, is itself the enterprise and adventure of the day. It is not an interval between more important matters, nor a duty to be crossed off a list, but the very centre of the day around which everything else is arranged. Each time he sets out, he seems to feel that something may happen, and very often something does.

If you would get exercise, Thoreau advises, go in search of the springs of life. He means the fresh sources of energy, beauty and wonder that bubble up in wild places, far from the gymnasium and the office. A spring is a beginning, and a walker who finds one has found a beginning of his own.

Think of a man swinging dumb-bells for his health, Thoreau says, while the springs of life are bubbling up in far-off pastures unsought by him. The comparison is comic, and it stings a little, because it describes so many of us who pay for exercise and forget the world outside the window. Somewhere, a meadow brook is running clear, and nobody has come to see it.

Moreover, he says, you must walk like a camel, which is said to be the only beast that ruminates when walking. To ruminate is to chew the cud, and also to turn a thought over and over in the mind, and Thoreau is happily playing on both meanings. The ideal walker, then, is a slow and patient animal, chewing the day's ideas as his feet carry him on.

When a traveller once asked Wordsworth's servant to show him her master's study, she answered, “Here is his library, but his study is out of doors.” Thoreau relishes the reply, for it contains much of his philosophy in a dozen words. The great thinking, it suggests, is done under the sky, and the books on the shelves are merely what is left of it.

William Wordsworth, the English poet, lived among the hills and lakes of northern England and was famous for his long walks. He is known to have made up many of his poems out of doors, murmuring the lines aloud as he went. Thoreau, who lived across the Atlantic, evidently admired a poet who did his best work on foot.

To walk like a camel, then, is to let your thoughts chew slowly on the day while your feet keep moving. The rhythm of the steps seems to loosen the knots of the mind, and many people find that a problem which defeated them at a desk will yield on a hillside. Thoreau would not have been surprised, for he trusted his legs to do much of his thinking.

So a walk, for Thoreau, is neither a medicine nor a task but an adventure, the day's own enterprise, undertaken by the whole person at once. The body provides the motion, the senses provide the world, and the mind, if it is wise, is content to follow and to notice. When all three set out together, he believes, a very ordinary afternoon becomes a small expedition into the unknown.

When Thoreau leaves the house, he does not wish to walk in a tidy, tamed countryside of clipped hedges and swept lanes. He wants to walk out into a Nature such as the old prophets and poets walked in, a country as wide and strange as the world was when the first stories were told. It is a high ambition for an afternoon, and he sets out each day as if it were within reach.

He names four of them, Menu, Moses, Homer and Chaucer, as if he were introducing old friends. Menu was a legendary lawgiver of ancient India, Moses a prophet and leader in the Bible, Homer the Greek poet of the Iliad, and Chaucer the English poet of the Middle Ages. The list reaches across thousands of years and many nations, and Thoreau enjoys the thought that all of them walked under the same open sky.

You may name it America, he says, but it is not America: neither Americus Vespucius, nor Columbus, nor the rest were the discoverers of it. The Nature that Thoreau means is older than any map or any name that explorers wrote upon it. His point is that the wild country he walks in cannot be claimed by a flag, because it was there long before the flags.

There is a truer account of this country in mythology, Thoreau declares, than in any history of America, so called, that he has seen. The old myths, as he reads them, remember the mystery and the power of the land, while histories tend to list its owners, its wars and its prices. It is a bold remark, and he leaves it standing for the reader to turn over.

Roads, in Thoreau's opinion, are made for horses and men of business, who want to get somewhere in a hurry and care little for what lies on either side. A road is a straight idea laid across the land: it joins one place to another and asks the traveller to ignore everything in between. The walker, who cares most about the country in between, finds it a poor guide for his purposes.

He confesses that he is not in a hurry to get to any tavern or grocery or livery-stable or depot, which are the places to which roads usually lead. The sort of man who wants to arrive somewhere will take the road; the sort who wants to be somewhere will leave it. Thoreau, as anyone who has read a few lines of him will guess, belongs firmly to the second kind.

I am a good horse to travel, he writes with a grin, but not from choice a roadster. He is willing to be useful, strong and steady on a long journey, but he does not wish to be harnessed to the highway like a cart-horse. Given his freedom, he would rather trot across the fields and pastures, taking his own line over the hills.

The landscape painter, Thoreau observes, uses the figures of men to mark a road in his picture. He would not, Thoreau adds with a smile, make that use of his figure, because he is never found walking in the road. A small man on a road makes the picture civilised, and Thoreau wishes to stand somewhere else.

To earn part of his living Thoreau worked as a land surveyor, measuring farms and woodlots for his neighbours, so he knew the fields, woods and boundary lines around Concord intimately. That knowledge gave him a hundred ways to cross the country without ever setting foot on the road. A man who has walked a farm's boundaries with a chain in his hands is not easily fenced in.

A field has no tavern at the end of it, and it asks nothing of the person who crosses it. The walker in a field is not on his way to anything; he is simply where he is, and the whole afternoon opens around him. That is the freedom Thoreau prefers to the freedom of the highway: the freedom of having nowhere to arrive.

Thoreau observes that in his own neighbourhood the best part of the land is not private property. The landscape is not owned, and so the walker enjoys a comparative freedom: he may usually cross a meadow, climb a hill or follow a brook without asking leave of anyone. It is a gift so common that his neighbours hardly notice it, and he is anxious that it should not be lost.

Yet he can imagine the day, perhaps not far off, when the whole landscape will be partitioned off into so-called pleasure-grounds, in which a few will take a narrow and exclusive pleasure. The word pleasure sounds generous, but the gates will be shut to everyone else, and the open country will shrink to a handful of private gardens. It is a gloomy forecast, but he delivers it in a calm and almost cheerful voice.

Fences will be multiplied, he warns, and man-traps and other engines invented to confine men to the public road, until walking over the surface of God's earth is construed to mean trespassing on some gentleman's grounds. The picture is a little comic, with traps in the hedgerows and fierce notices on the gates, and in some form it has come true in many places. Where land is closed, the path becomes a corridor and the walker a prisoner of the road.

To enjoy a thing exclusively, Thoreau says, is commonly to exclude yourself from the true enjoyment of it. A person who walls off a piece of landscape for his own use shuts out his neighbours, and he may also shut out the very pleasure he hoped to keep. We can test the idea ourselves: a view that is shared with a friend is often better than the same view enjoyed alone.

Let us improve our opportunities, then, he says, before the evil days come, and enjoy the open land while we may. The advice is urgent but cheerful: use the open fields while they are still open, and walk through them as freely as if the right might not last. It is advice that readers have been taking, and needing, ever since his essay first appeared in print.

Some countries today protect the right to walk across open country in their laws, with sensible limits. In Scotland and Sweden and Norway, for example, people may roam over much open land on foot, provided that they behave with care and respect the land and its owners. Thoreau, who feared the multiplying fences, might well have approved, and so might many a walker today.

Thoreau's own walks took him along the Concord River, over the Great Meadows and up Fair Haven Hill, a landscape that he knew in every season and every kind of weather. These were not wild places in the sense of the far west; they were farms, pastures and woodlots, shaped by human hands. Yet he found wildness in them, in the edge of a swamp or the fall of the light.

He believes that the country within about ten miles of his home, which is the distance of an afternoon's walk, could fill a lifetime of walks. A lifetime of about seventy years, he suggests, would still not be long enough to use it up, so rich is any piece of ground to someone who looks. It is a cheerful thought for anyone who feels that adventure is always somewhere else.

Even the nearest fields, Thoreau found, never became quite the same twice, for the seasons and the weather kept changing them. In his journal he noted the dates when flowers opened, when ice melted and when birds returned, and those dates were never exactly the same from one year to the next. To the person who looks closely, familiar ground is a story with a different chapter every day.

A walker with open eyes, Thoreau suggests, is never short of new places, even in his own back yard. The countryside is a book that can be read again and again, and each reading turns up something that was missed before. That is why a person who goes out every day, as he did, can grow richer without ever travelling far from home.

Thoreau now asks a question that every walker knows: what is it that makes it so hard, sometimes, to decide where we will walk? We stand at the door with the whole countryside before us, and we hesitate like a traveller at a crossroads, though nothing is at stake but an afternoon. The delay is comic, but he treats it as a sign of something deeper.

His answer is a hopeful one: he believes that there is a subtle magnetism in Nature, which, if we unconsciously yield to it, will direct us aright. The pull is faint, and it is easily drowned out by habit, by hurry and by the opinions of other people. A walker who has quieted his mind, however, may feel it as clearly as a needle feels the north.

It is not indifferent to us, he says, which way we walk, and he means it quite seriously. There is a right way, but from heedlessness and stupidity we are very liable to take the wrong one. The thought is odd, as if the countryside were a piece of music that could be played in the right key or the wrong.

We would like, he says, to take that walk never yet taken by us through this actual world, a walk perfectly symbolical of the path we love to travel in our ideal inner world. In such a walk every turning would seem to answer a question of the heart, and the destination would be the place we most wished to reach. Few walks ever quite live up to that dream, but the dream is what sends us out of the door.

Sometimes, no doubt, we find it hard to choose our direction, and Thoreau offers a gentle explanation. It is because the path does not yet exist distinctly in our idea, he says: we cannot take a road that we have not yet imagined. The restless hesitation at the door is, in this view, the mind drawing a map before the feet can follow it.

A compass needle is a good picture of this inner pull, and he returns to the image in a moment. It points north because the Earth itself acts like an enormous magnet, and a needle that is free to turn will find that direction without being told. Thoreau suggests that the human spirit has a little needle of its own, and that it swings quietly toward the places where it will thrive.

When Thoreau goes out of the house for a walk, uncertain as yet where he will bend his steps, he submits to his instinct to decide for him. He does not consult a map or a clock, and he has no plan beyond waiting to feel which way he is drawn. It is a very simple method, and as we shall see, it gives him a surprisingly steady answer.

Sometimes, he admits, he turns round and round, irresolute, for a quarter of an hour. He faces one way and then another, weighing the hills against the woods, and nothing seems to decide the matter. Anyone who has stood on a doorstep with a free afternoon and no plan will know exactly how he feels.

It may seem strange and whimsical, he admits, to let instinct decide such a matter, but he finds that the choice, when it finally comes, is neither random nor weak. It arrives with a kind of quiet force, as though the afternoon itself had made up his mind for him. A man who learns to wait for that signal, he implies, will seldom go far wrong.

So the first act of every walk, for Thoreau, is a small act of listening. Before the first step he waits, with his stick in his hand and his eyes on the horizon, to feel where the day wants him to go. The habit is worth borrowing, since it turns the doorway into a place of attention rather than of hurry.

When Thoreau lets his instinct decide, he finds, strange and whimsical as it may seem, that he finally and inevitably settles on the southwest. He heads for some particular wood or meadow or deserted pasture or hill in that direction. The pull is steady, like a habit, and it returns him again and again to the same favourite corners of the countryside.

His needle, as he calls it, is slow in settling, and it varies a few degrees, nor does it always point due southwest. It has good authority for its variations, he says, yet it always settles somewhere between west and south-southwest. Like a real compass, it wavers and trembles for a moment, and then comes to rest on the same general bearing.

The future lies that way for him, Thoreau says, and the earth on that side seems more unexhausted and richer. He is speaking about farmland and forest, but he is speaking about hope as well: the west is where he expects something new to begin. In his mind, each afternoon's walk is a small journey into tomorrow, and the setting sun marks the direction.

The outline that would bound his walks, he says, would not be a circle but a parabola, or rather one of those cometary orbits which have been thought to be non-returning curves. In this case the curve opens westward, and his house occupies the place of the sun. The picture is half astronomy and half joke, and it makes his habit of walking west sound like a law of the universe.

Some comets, it was thought, travel along curves that never bring them home; they sweep past the sun and vanish into the dark. Thoreau borrows the thought for his own wanderings, which seem to him to leave the house behind as if they meant never to return. In practice he came back every evening, yet the spirit of the image is that of the crusader who does not look back.

He puts his whole preference into a single line: Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free. A walk toward the west feels like his own free choice, while a walk toward the east feels like a duty laid on him by someone else. The two directions weigh differently on the spirit, and he claims to feel the difference at once.

No business leads him westward, and he is not excited by the prospect of a walk to the east. It is hard for him to believe that he will find fair landscapes, or sufficient wildness and freedom, behind the eastern horizon. To the east lay Boston, the great city, and the old settled world; to the west lay open ground and the chance of surprise.

He believes that the forest which he sees on the western horizon stretches uninterruptedly toward the setting sun, and that there are no towns or cities in it of enough consequence to disturb him. It is a belief rather than a fact, and he holds it the way a child holds a map of a country it has never visited. Beyond the last hill, in his mind, the trees simply go on and on until they meet the setting sun.

Let me live where I will, Thoreau writes, on this side is the city, on that the wilderness, and ever I am leaving the city more and more, and withdrawing into the wilderness. Wherever he stands, in other words, there is a direction that leads toward the wild, and he always takes it. His walks, added together, form one long and happy departure from the crowd and its business.

He would not lay so much stress on this fact, he says, if he did not believe that something like it is the prevailing tendency of his countrymen. I must walk toward Oregon, he declares, and not toward Europe, and he says it as plainly as a man giving his address. In his day thousands of settlers were heading west, and Thoreau felt the same pull working quietly in a single walker.

That way the nation is moving, Thoreau says, and he goes further: mankind, in his view, progresses from east to west. It is a sweeping claim, stated as plainly as a weather report, and it rests on nothing more than the habit of the sun and the movement of the people of his day. Modern readers may smile at its confidence, but they will recognise the restless spirit behind it.

In his day there was plenty of evidence to support the claim, for the whole country seemed to be on the move. Settlers had long since crossed the Appalachian mountains and the Mississippi River, and from 1843 great wagon trains set out each spring along the trail to Oregon, carrying whole families and everything they owned. To a man looking at a map of the young nation, everything seemed to be tilting toward the sunset.

Today we must add something that Thoreau does not stop to say in this part of his essay. The lands to the west were not empty, for Native nations had lived there for thousands of years, and the westward movement that he describes took the land and the freedom of many of them. His essay is a fine piece of nature writing, but it speaks with the voice of a settler's nation, and an honest reader keeps that in mind.

We go eastward, he says, to realize history and study the works of art and literature, retracing the steps of the race. An eastward walker is a scholar of the past, who finds his answers in museums, libraries and ruins. Such a journey has its value, but Thoreau cannot feel that it leads him anywhere new.

We go westward, on the other hand, as into the future, with a spirit of enterprise and adventure. The west is where a person goes to make something new, to plant a field or to found a town, rather than to study what others have already made. For a walker with Thoreau's temperament, the choice between past and future is made by the compass in his chest.

The Atlantic, Thoreau says, is a Lethe, in our passage over which we have had an opportunity to forget the Old World and its institutions. Many of his countrymen were, after all, immigrants or the children of immigrants, and many of them had crossed that wide water hoping to begin again. To forget, in this sense, is not a loss but a liberty, a chance to leave old quarrels, old ranks and old habits behind.

Lethe is the river of forgetting in Greek myth, and the poets imagined the dead drinking its waters so that they would forget their earlier lives. By borrowing the name for the Atlantic, Thoreau suggests that the voyage across it washed the memory of the old country away. It is a rich image, though a sad one if you think of what the travellers left behind.

If we do not succeed this time, he says, there is perhaps one more chance before the human race reaches the banks of the Styx: the Lethe of the Pacific, which he calls three times as wide. The Styx, in Greek myth, is the river of the dead, so he is joking that humankind has two oceans in which to forget its mistakes. The tone is playful, but the worry underneath is real: a civilization may need many tries to learn its lessons.

The younger Michaux, a French botanist who travelled west of the Alleghanies in 1802, reported that the common question among the newly settled people was, “From what part of the world have you come?” It was as if those vast and fertile regions were the natural meeting place and common country of all the inhabitants of the globe. Thoreau enjoys the picture of a land where people from every country meet and begin again.

To use an obsolete Latin word, he says, he might put it this way: Ex Oriente lux; ex Occidente FRUX. In plain English, that means light from the East and fruit from the West, wisdom on one side and harvest on the other. Thoreau is a man who would rather taste the harvest than reread the old lessons.

As he walks west, Thoreau recalls an old dream of the poets and storytellers. They imagined that somewhere beyond the setting sun, across the ocean that ended the known world, there lay a golden country of ease and plenty. The dream is as old as the habit of watching the sun go down and wondering what it leaves behind.

The Greeks told of the Hesperides, nymphs who guarded a tree of golden apples in a garden at the western edge of the world. Their name is linked to a Greek word for evening, the hour when the sun sinks into the sea and the west turns to fire. In that garden, the old tale suggests, the golden fruit ripened beyond the reach of ordinary people.

One of the labours of the hero Heracles was to fetch some of those golden apples, and the tale takes him to the farthest edge of the known world. In some versions he meets giants and a watchful dragon, for treasure in the west is never easy to win. The Greeks pictured the western edge of the world as a place of danger, beauty and reward, much as Thoreau pictures the western woods.

The philosopher Plato described another western land, the island of Atlantis, a rich and powerful place that sank beneath the waves in a single day and night. Nobody has ever found evidence that it really existed, and most scholars treat it as a story invented to make a point about pride and power. Even so, it has haunted the human imagination for more than two thousand years, and it still does.

The Greek poets also pictured the Elysian Fields, a blessed country at the edge of the world where heroes were said to rest in gentle weather after their labours. Like the Hesperides, it was often imagined in the far west, where the sun goes down and the day's work ends. All these golden places share one feature: they are somewhere else, beyond the horizon, and a person must travel to reach them.

Thoreau likes to imagine that these old poets were dreaming of the very land in which he lives. A country of wide forests, fresh soil and room to grow could, in his fancy, be the golden island that they had in mind. It is a pleasing thought for a man who has walked so many afternoons toward the setting sun, and it turns every western hill into a piece of ancient legend.

Columbus, too, looked to the west, and in 1492 he sailed out across the Atlantic in search of a new route to Asia. Instead he reached islands of the Americas that were new to Europeans, and a new age of exploration and conquest began. The voyage proved how powerfully the western horizon can draw a person on, though the consequences for the peoples already living there were severe.

A line by the Irish bishop George Berkeley, written about 1726, says that the course of empire moves westward. Many Americans of Thoreau's day knew it well, and it matched the way they pictured their own future as a nation. The sentiment was grand, but Thoreau cared less for empires than for the wild country that lay in their path.

A walker who goes west in the afternoon has the setting sun in front of him, and his shadow stretches out behind him toward home. As the hours pass the shadow grows longer, the light grows redder and the whole landscape seems to warm up like a coal in a fire. It is not hard to see why a man who loved evening light would choose to face that way.

So for Thoreau, walking west means walking into the light, toward the best hours of the day. The habit has a practical side, since an afternoon walker who heads west keeps the evening glow before his eyes. It has a poetic side as well, for a man who walks toward the sunset is always, in some small way, walking toward hope.

Thoreau now makes a cheerful claim about the sky above his own country, with evident pleasure. The heavens of America, he says, appear to him infinitely higher, and the stars brighter. The remark comes almost as a boast, and he makes it with the confidence of a man who has spent more evenings under the open sky than most of his neighbours.

He trusts that these facts are symbolical of the height to which the philosophy, poetry and religion of the American people may one day soar. The sky, in other words, is a sign and a promise of what the human mind can reach, if it is given room. A cramped and smoky place, he implies, makes cramped and smoky thoughts, while open air makes room for larger ones.

At length, he hopes, the immaterial heaven will appear as much higher to the American mind, and the signs that star it as much brighter. By the immaterial heaven he means the inner sky of thought and belief, in which ideas shine like constellations. His wish is that the country's writers, thinkers and believers will one day look up into a broader sky of the spirit.

He believes that climate reacts on a person, for there is something in mountain air that feeds the spirit and inspires. Anyone who has climbed a hill on a clear morning, with the lungs full and the eye reaching far, may well agree with him. Thoreau does not offer proof, only the hope that the open sky has an effect on the thoughts of those who live beneath it.

Will a person, he asks, grow to greater perfection intellectually as well as physically under these influences? Or is it unimportant how many foggy days there are in his life, after all? The second question is meant lightly, yet it carries a real thought: the weather of a place enters the minds of those who live there.

I trust that we shall be more imaginative, he writes, that our thoughts will be clearer, fresher and more ethereal, as our sky. Ethereal means light and airy, as if made of the same stuff as the air, and Thoreau wants a mind that is as free and transparent as a spring morning. It is an attractive ideal, and a hard one to live up to in a busy week.

He hopes that the American understanding will be broader, like the plains, and the intellect of its people on a grander scale, like its thunder and lightning, its rivers, mountains and forests. The comparison is typical of Thoreau, who treats the landscape as a teacher of the mind. A person raised among great horizons, he suggests, ought to think in great sweeps rather than small steps.

Last of all, he hopes that the hearts of its people will match in breadth and depth and grandeur the inland seas of the continent. The inland seas are the Great Lakes, so vast that a person on one shore cannot see across, and their storms have wrecked many ships. It is the finest thing he can wish for the human heart: to be as wide and as deep as a lake with no far shore.

He then asks two large questions: else to what end does the world go on, and why was America discovered? If the new world does not bring a new height of mind and a new breadth of heart, he suggests, then the whole long adventure of discovery was hardly worth the trouble. The questions are asked with a smile, but they are not a joke, for they show what he cares about most.

Of course, the same stars shine over every land, and Thoreau's claim about the American sky is a poet's boast as much as a fact. Yet stars do look brighter from a dark place far from lamps and cities, and that is a pleasure any walker can test on a clear night. Where it is safe, stand in an open field after dark, let your eyes adjust for a quarter of an hour, and the sky will begin to feel a good deal higher.

Thoreau now asks for something far stronger than a pleasant park or a tidy garden. Give me a wildness, he cries, whose glance no civilization can endure, whose very look would make a town lower its eyes. The wish is for a nature so strong that no amount of fences, laws or good manners could ever subdue it.

He adds, with a grin, that this wildness should be as strong as if we lived on the marrow of koodoos devoured raw. A koodoo, now usually spelled kudu, is a large African antelope with spiral horns, and the image is meant to shock a polite audience. Thoreau, who lived on plain food at Walden, is joking about a diet of pure wild strength.

Hope and the future for him, Thoreau says, are not in lawns and cultivated fields, not in towns and cities, but in the impervious and quaking swamps. It is a surprising place to look for hope, since most people think of swamps as dirty, dangerous and useless. He thinks of them as the last wild store of life in a country that is being steadily drained and ploughed.

When he once examined his liking for a farm he had thought of buying, he found that he was attracted solely by a few square rods of unfathomable bog in one corner. That was the jewel which dazzled him, he says: not the good fields or the fine barn, but the wet and hopeless corner that no plough could use. It is a joke at the expense of every buyer who has ever been charmed by the wrong thing, and it is also an honest confession.

He derives more of his subsistence, he says, from the swamps around his native town than from the cultivated gardens of the village. He is not speaking of potatoes, but of the food of the spirit: the wonder, the quiet and the sense of the untouched that a swamp gives to anyone who goes into it. The gardens feed the body, and the swamps, in his view, feed the rest.

There are no richer flower beds in his eyes than the dense beds of dwarf andromeda that cover these tender places on the earth's surface. The plant is a low shrub of bogs, with rows of small white bell-shaped flowers in spring, and its scientific name in his day was Cassandra calyculata. To most walkers it is a modest thing, but Thoreau admires it as another man might admire a bed of roses.

Botany, he admits, can go no further than telling him the names of the shrubs that grow in such places: the high blueberry, panicled andromeda, lambkill, azalea and rhodora, all standing in the quaking sphagnum. Names are useful, but they are only the beginning of knowing a place, and he wants the feeling of it as well. A visitor may label every plant in the swamp and still have missed the swamp.

The moss that floors such places is called sphagnum, and it can hold remarkable amounts of water, like a vast green sponge. That is why the ground of a bog quakes under a walker's boots, and why a careless step may take him in up to the knee. Thoreau knew the danger and went in anyway, though a sensible walker takes care and keeps to safe ground.

He enters a swamp, he says, as a sacred place, a sanctum sanctorum, the Latin name for the holiest chamber of a temple. There, in the dark and the wet, is the strength, the marrow of Nature. A reader smiles at the grandness of it, and then remembers that most of us have never entered a swamp with such respect.

The wild wood covers the virgin mould, he writes, and the same soil is good for men and for trees. The ground that grows a forest, he means, can grow a strong person too, if the person will only live close to it. It is a hopeful idea, for it suggests that a healthy life and a healthy wood depend on the same living ground.

A man's health, Thoreau says, requires as many acres of meadow in his prospect as his farm requires loads of muck. The comparison is typically earthy: muck is farm manure, and just as a field must be fed to give a crop, a person must be fed by wide and open views. The idea is his own, and it is offered as an opinion, not as a medical rule.

A wide view of untamed meadow is, for him, a kind of food for the eyes and the spirit. There are the strong meats, he says, on which a person feeds, and a diet of lawns and clipped hedges is thin by comparison. Anyone who has felt the mind loosen on seeing an open field, with no building in sight, knows what he means.

A town is saved, he declares, not more by the righteous men in it than by the woods and swamps that surround it. It is a surprising thing to say at a time when many people saw woods mainly as timber and future farmland. Thoreau sees the surrounding wild as a kind of guardian, quietly protecting the town from its own narrowness.

A township where one primitive forest waves above, he says, while another primitive forest rots below, is fitted to raise not only corn and potatoes, but poets and philosophers for the coming ages. The living trees above and the fallen ones below together make the rich dark soil, and the soil, in turn, makes room for greater things than crops. His picture is of a community whose ground is alive, and whose people are fed in mind as well as in body.

In such soil, he says, grew Homer and Confucius and the rest, and out of such a wilderness comes the Reformer eating locusts and wild honey. He is naming the great poets and teachers of the old world and the prophets of the desert, and he places them all in the same wild ground. Greatness of mind, he suggests, has often grown at the edge of the village, not in its centre.

Homer was the Greek poet of the Iliad, and Confucius was a Chinese teacher who lived about twenty-five centuries ago. The Reformer eating locusts and wild honey is John the Baptist, who, according to the Bible, preached in the desert before Jesus began his own teaching. Thoreau's list is respectful to all three, and it treats the wilderness as the common birthplace of many of the world's great voices.

Life consists with wildness, he says, and the most alive is the wildest, whether it is a tree, a fox or a person. A wild thing is not yet subdued to man, and its presence refreshes him, as a cold stream refreshes a walker who has been long in the sun. In a world of fences and schedules, a glimpse of a free animal or an untrimmed tree is a kind of tonic.

In another essay, written after a journey into the Maine woods, he asked why the nation should not keep wild preserves where the bear and the panther might still live. It was a remarkable thought for his time, long before the first national park was founded in the United States. Today, in many countries, large areas of wild land are protected, and his words are often quoted by those who work to protect them.

A person who pressed forward without rest, who made endless demands on life and grew fast, would always find himself in a new country or wilderness, surrounded by the raw material of life. He would be climbing over the prostrate stems of primitive forest trees, as a pioneer does. The thought is that growth and wildness belong together, and that a mind which keeps moving will never run out of untouched ground.

Everything he has said so far leads to one famous line: in Wildness is the preservation of the World. He does not say that wildness is pleasant, or pretty, or good for a holiday; he says that the world itself is preserved by it. The sentence has been quoted so often, in so many books and speeches, that it is now almost a motto of the movement to protect wild places.

The civilized nations, Thoreau says, Greece, Rome and England, have been sustained by the primitive forests which anciently rotted where they stand. Their farms and cities, their schools and their libraries, all rest on the dark soil that those forests slowly made. He sees a civilization as a late and fragile flower growing out of a much older wildness.

Such nations survive, he says, only so long as the soil is not exhausted, and little is to be expected of a nation that must make manure of the bones of its fathers. In such a land the poet lives only on the fat that he stored up before, and the philosopher comes down on his marrow-bones. The image is grim and comic together, and it describes a culture that has used up its own capital.

The founders of every state which has risen to eminence, Thoreau says, have drawn their nourishment and vigour from a similar wild source. A people begins on rough ground, in forests and on frontiers, where it must be strong and clever to survive. Only later, when it grows comfortable, does it forget where its strength came from.

According to the Roman legend, the twin founders of Rome, Romulus and Remus, were abandoned as babies and suckled by a she-wolf. Thoreau seizes on the old tale and makes it a lesson: a people is strongest when it has been nursed by something wild. The comparison is a thoughtful use of legend, though it should be read as a poet's argument rather than as history.

It was because the children of the Empire were not suckled by the wolf, he says, that they were conquered and displaced by the children of the northern forests, who were. Historians give many reasons for the fall of Rome, and most of them are less poetic, but his picture is a vivid one. It gives the old story of a tired empire and its vigorous neighbours a moral about wildness.

In literature, too, he says, it is only the wild that attracts us, and he does not say it apologetically. Dulness is but another name for tameness, and a tame book is one that has been written to please and not to startle. A reader with a long evening ahead should choose, he implies, the book with a little danger in it.

It is the uncivilized, free and wild thinking in Hamlet and the Iliad, in all the Scriptures and mythologies, not learned in the schools, that delights us. Shakespeare's prince, Homer's heroes and the old sacred stories were not written to be tidy; they speak out of a world larger than any classroom. That is why they do not wear out, though readers have returned to them for hundreds and even thousands of years.

As the wild duck is more swift and beautiful than the tame, so is the wild thought, the mallard of the mind, which wings its way above the fens in the falling dew. The mallard is the wild ancestor of most farmyard ducks, and it is stronger, quicker and handsomer than any of its fat descendants. Thoreau wants his reader to look for such thoughts the way a patient observer watches wild birds, with quiet and with luck.

A truly good book, he says, is something as natural, and as unexpectedly and unaccountably fair and perfect, as a wild flower discovered on the prairies of the West or in the jungles of the East. Even its author could hardly explain it; it seems to have grown rather than been made, and the reader is grateful. Such books are rare, which is why we remember the day on which we found one.

Genius, he says, is a light which makes the darkness visible, like the lightning's flash, which perchance shatters the temple of knowledge itself. It is not a taper lighted at the hearth-stone of the race, which pales before the light of common day. A candle is a comfort, but a flash of lightning shows the whole landscape at once, and that is the kind of light he values in writing.

In Thoreau's opinion, English literature from the days of the minstrels to the Lake Poets, Chaucer and Spenser and Milton, and even Shakespeare, included, breathes no quite fresh and, in this sense, wild strain. He finds it an essentially tame and civilized literature, reflecting Greece and Rome rather than the woods outside the window. It is a bold judgment, and one that most readers will want to argue with.

England's wilderness, he says, is a green wood, and its wild man is a Robin Hood. The outlaw of the old ballads is lively and likeable, but he is a friendly, storybook figure, a long way from the real wild. Thoreau wanted something harsher and stranger, a nature that does not know it is being written about.

There is plenty of genial love of Nature in these writers, he allows, but not so much of Nature herself. They like a pleasant prospect from a window or a walk by a gentle stream, and they praise it in graceful verse. He wants the weather, the mud, the thorns and the wind, the whole rough thing and not only its pretty face.

Alexander von Humboldt was a famous German naturalist and explorer, and Thoreau says that the science of Humboldt is one thing and poetry is another. Despite all the discoveries of science and the accumulated learning of mankind, he says, the poet today enjoys no advantage over Homer. Facts can be added to forever, but the gift of seeing and saying them truly does not grow with the pile.

Where, he asks, is the literature which gives true expression to Nature, and not merely a lover's praise of her? He would be a poet who could impress the winds and streams into his service, to speak for him. The ambition is enormous, and it lies behind much of what Thoreau wrote about a pond, a woodchuck or a patch of snow.

Such a poet, he says, would nail words to their primitive senses, as farmers drive down stakes in the spring which the frost has heaved. Over a winter the frost lifts fence stakes out of the soil, and in the same way words drift away from their first meanings, until they need to be hammered home again. The best writers, he suggests, keep going back to the plain original sense of a word and make it mean something again.

He would also derive his words afresh each time he used them, transplanting them into his writing with earth adhering to their roots. A wild plant lifted carefully on a spade, with its soil still around it, survives the move, and a word treated the same way keeps its life. The reader, opening such a book, feels a little of the field come in with the sentence.

His words would be so true and fresh and natural that they would appear to expand like the buds at the approach of spring, though they lay half smothered between two musty leaves in a library. Printed words, he implies, are usually pressed flat and dry, like flowers in an album, and a great writer can make them swell with life again. Reading such lines on a winter evening, one almost expects to smell the soil.

They would bloom and bear fruit there, after their kind, annually, for the faithful reader, in sympathy with surrounding Nature. The picture is of a book that works like an orchard: each spring it flowers again, and each year it gives a fresh crop of meaning to anyone who returns. Many readers say that Walden is like that, and so, perhaps, is this essay.

Thoreau tried hard to write in just this way, and many readers think he succeeded. His journal, kept day after day in the fields and by the river, is full of sentences written close to the moment of seeing, with a little of the soil still on them. The habit of taking notes outdoors is one that any walker can borrow, with a pencil and a small book.

Thoreau closes his essay with a memory of a late afternoon in November, after a cold and grey day, when the sky had hung low over the fields for hours. He was walking across a meadow at the edge of a wood, in the plain mood of a man taking the same walk he had taken many times before. Nothing about the hour suggested that it would become the closing picture of his essay.

Then, low in the sky, the sun broke through, and the whole afternoon was changed in a moment. After hours of dull cloud the light came in sideways, flat and gold, and it seemed to Thoreau that the world had been given back to him. Such sudden gifts of weather are one of the great rewards of being out of doors.

The softest, brightest light fell on the dry grass blades, on the stems of the trees in the wood, and on the leaves of the shrub oaks on the hillside opposite. Everything it touched seemed to glow from within, like a lamp behind a paper shade, though the grass was brown and the leaves were dead. It is the light of late autumn, low and long and kind, which flatters even the plainest landscape.

Every tree and shrub threw a long shadow across the meadow, stretching away from the setting sun as far as the eye could follow. The grass between the shadows was lit so brightly that the dark and the bright lay side by side like the stripes of a cloth. The whole scene had the stillness of a picture, yet it was alive with warmth.

The air was so warm and calm, Thoreau felt, that nothing was wanting to make a paradise of that meadow. It is an extraordinary thing to say about a field in a New England November, and yet readers who have stood in such a light will not doubt him. For a few minutes the ordinary place became the Holy Land he had been talking about all through the essay.

In New England in late November the sun sets before half past four, so such light is brief, and it begins to fade almost as soon as it is noticed. A walker has only a short time to enjoy it before the cold and the dark come back. That brevity is part of its beauty, and part of the reason that he remembered it so carefully.

Such an evening, he implies, comes without notice, and it is seen only by someone who is out of doors and awake to it. The people at their desks and counters, sitting with the lamps lit, will never know that it happened. This is the reward that Thoreau means when he says that a walk is the enterprise and adventure of the day.

So, he ends, we saunter toward the Holy Land, and the word saunter returns at the very end, as a bell returns to its first note. The Holy Land is not a place where we arrive and stop; it is the direction in which we keep walking, and the pleasure lies in the walking. Thoreau's opening promised an art of sauntering, and his closing lines show that the art is a way of hope.

Till one day, he hopes, the sun shall shine more brightly than ever he has done, and shall perchance shine into our minds and hearts. The sun that shone on the meadow is the picture; the thing pictured is understanding, a clear light by which a person sees life whole. It is a hope offered with great gentleness, as if he did not wish to claim more than he knew.

That light will light up our whole lives, he says, with a great awakening light, as warm and serene and golden as on a bank-side in autumn. The last word of the essay is therefore a picture, not an argument: a grassy slope in the low sun, with nothing to prove and nothing to be done. After so much talk of wildness, swamps and crusades, it ends in a quiet, golden peace.

Thoreau is buried in Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in Concord, on a wooded ridge near his friends Emerson and Hawthorne, and not far from the Alcott family. His own headstone is small and plain, and it carries a single word, his first name, as if the rest were already in his books. Visitors often leave pencils and small notes beside it, a fitting tribute for a pencil-maker's son.

His book Walden, printed in 1854, was not widely read at first, and a first printing of two thousand copies took years to sell. In the century and a half since, it has become one of the best-loved books in American writing, and Walking is often read beside it. Both works carry the same gentle dare: slow down, look closely and ask what you really need.

Later nature writers shared his love of wild places and said so in their own voices. John Muir, the Scottish-born naturalist who founded the Sierra Club in 1892, wrote that wildness is a necessity, a claim that Thoreau would have recognised at once. Their books helped to build the idea, now familiar, that wild land is a treasure that people should protect for one another.

In 1964 the United States passed the Wilderness Act, a law that protects large areas of wild land and describes wilderness as a place where nature is left free and people are only visitors. Its language carries an echo of Thoreau's old argument, though he could not have imagined such a law. Many other countries have since made their own promises to protect their wild places, in laws and in parks.

Thoreau's lesson is that you do not need a vast wilderness to feel the wild. A field, a stream or a city park may be enough, if you bring your whole attention to it, for wildness is partly a matter of how we look. A weed in a pavement crack, a hawk over a rooftop and a dawn chorus of birds in a hedge are all pieces of it.

Try a short saunter of your own, with no destination, no hurry and, if you can manage it, no phone. Walk slowly, leave your errands and your worries behind as far as you can, and let your senses do the work. If your mind runs back to the office, as Thoreau's did, simply bring it gently back to the sounds and smells around you.

Carry a small notebook, as he did, and write down what you notice: the first flower of spring, the colour of the evening sky, the call of a bird you cannot name. Over a year those small notes will become a record of your own place, and they will teach you more about it than any guidebook. Thoreau suggests that attention is a kind of ownership that no fence can take away.

Walking is also widely recommended today as a gentle and low-cost way for most people to stay active. Many health organizations suggest that most adults aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, and a brisk walk counts toward that goal. How much is right for you, however, depends on your age, your health and your circumstances.

Thoreau was a writer and not a doctor, and his remarks about health, from his four hours a day to his trust in wild air, are his own opinions. Nobody should assume that a walk can cure an illness or replace proper care. If you have a health condition or any doubt about exercise, ask a doctor or another qualified professional before you begin.

This book retells Thoreau's essay and offers general information about his ideas, and it is not medical advice, so please speak to a doctor or another health professional about your own needs. Walk gently, within your own limits, and let the open air do what it can for you. When you next step through your own door, remember his line that in Wildness is the preservation of the World, and take a good long saunter to see for yourself.
